papers.title: Making Human-AI Contributions Transparent in Qualitative Coding
papers.authors: Buffalo, USA, June 10-14
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools offer  promise in facilitating code discovery, refinement, and large -scale analyses in qualitative coding. While prior work has focused on the feasibility of AI tools, limited research has examined the process of human -AI collaboration in qualitative coding tasks. In this paper, we present a self-study that details how we use GPT -4, a generative AI tool, to assist with the early stages of inductive qualitative coding. We conduct two analyses that highlight human-AI collaboration: (1) how AI integration augments the coding workflow, as researchers iterate between reading data, open coding, refining, and organizing codes, and (2) how AI’s output contributes to the development and refinement of the codebook. These visualizations aim to improve the transparency and trustworthiness of AI-integrated qualitative coding. They illustrate how to apply insights from collaborative learning research to explore human-AI collaboration.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Making Human-AI Contributions Transparent in Qualitative Coding Saríah Lopez-Fierro. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Use of Generative AI for Boundary Crossing in Interdisciplinary
papers.authors: Collaborative Research, Shotaro Naganuma, Tsubasa Minematsu, Kana Matsueda, Jun Oshima
papers.abstract: Ph.D. students in interdisciplinary education programs face challenges in achieving effective collaboration. To support them in overcoming their challenges, we  designed a workshop using generative artificial intelligence ( AI) as a broker device to create  partially shared objects  for boundary crossing. In the workshop, groups of students collaborated  by coordinating research themes proposed by ChatGPT with the input of  their research information. After their collaboration, experts evaluated improvements in the proposed themes. We then analyzed four high-outcome and three low -outcome groups to identify key discourse moves for successful knowledge-building discourse. Epistemic Network Analysis  (ENA) and discourse analysis  revealed that  compared to low -outcome groups, high- outcome groups actively enhanced explanations , connected/synthesized their discourse, and shared relevant disciplinary domain and research-design knowledge to improve their themes without persisting with those that they initially judged as non -promising. We utilized these results to propose a conjecture map toward future systematic design-based research on interdisciplinary education.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Use of Generative AI for Boundary Crossing in Interdisciplinary Collaborative Research. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Shall We Play a Game? Distributed Games with a Generative AI Player
papers.authors: Jenna Matthews, Ha Nguyen, Hillary Swanson
papers.abstract: The prevalence of generative AI tools – especially large language models that enable human-like conversation – provides an opportunity to study how human learners interact with AI as collaborative ideators in the learning process. We expand the framework of distributed games (which initially focused on epistemic games of discovery as distributed processes) to investigate learner interaction with generative AI in design tasks. Through a comparative case study of two undergraduates using a generative AI tool in design tasks, we illustrate different ways in which learners orient themselves to the elements of the game (task, form, other players, etc.) and the corresponding complexity of the game played. We discuss implications for the design of learning environments that facilitate interaction with AI tools in distributed creativ e tasks.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Shall We Play a Game? Distributed Games with a Generative AI Player Jenna Matthews. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: A Knowledge Building-Modeling Approach to Scientific Inquiry
papers.authors: Dina Soliman, Xueqi Feng
papers.abstract: This study explores how a Knowledge  Building - Modeling approach (KBM) was used to enhance grade 5  students’ understanding of dynamic mechanisms related to natural hazards. Forty-three students collectively engaged in an iterative KBM process involving idea- driven discourse on Knowledge Forum. Additionally, students created models in response to emerging theories and questions. I terations were driven by students’ discourse and supported by learning analytics to advance idea and model building . Results show that students  engaged in deeper discourse practices  over time. T heir models increasingly reflected complex causal reasoning and their knowledge of natural hazards improved. Analysis revealed that knowledge building discourse was a good predictor of both scientific understanding and modeling practices. We discuss the work that informed our intervention and highlight the KBM approach. Implications of designing knowledge building environments enriched with modeling to promote complex reasoning and modeling practices are discussed.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: A Knowledge Building-Modeling Approach to Scientific Inquiry. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Using Pose Data to Explore Changes in Students’ Self-Efficacy and Community Belonging in Makerspaces
papers.authors: Bertrand Schneider, Edwin Chng, epitomize this philosophy, by encouraging community-based, project-oriented learning through, learning environments, while others do not, learning and teaching.
papers.abstract: Constructionist learning (Papert, 1980) can be a powerful way of fostering students’ self-efficacy and their connection to a community. Makerspaces and digital fabrication labs epitomize this philosophy, by encouraging community-based, project-oriented learning through the creation of both physical and digital products. Because makerspaces are open-ended, messy learning environments, understanding why some students have transformative experienc es, while others do not, remains a challenge. In this paper, we explore how multimodal learning analytics can provide a complementary lens to quantify and visualize students’ learning trajectories. We collected students’ 3D poses from video data collected during a semester-long course and used unsupervised machine learning approaches to identify behavioral states. We present preliminary correlational results with students’ reports of self -efficacy and community belonging. We discuss these findings and how they could be used to support constructionist learning and teaching.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Using Pose Data to Explore Changes in Students’ Self-Efficacy and Community Belonging in Makerspaces. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Learning Under Stress: Enhancing Team-Based Simulation Training with Multimodal Data
papers.authors: Daniel Sánchez
papers.abstract: High-stakes healthcare environments present unique stress challenges impacting individual performance and collaborative dynamics. This study harnesses multimodal learning analytics to investigate stress patterns in team -based nursing simulations, using medical -grade sensors to map physiological stress responses to key collaborative events, like decision-making during patient health crises. Analysis revealed that participants' stress levels not only peaked during high-responsibility tasks but also showed elevated baselines, suggesting pre -simulation stress. Integrating these findings i nto reflective debriefing sessions can enhance stress management and support deeper learning. This research highlights the value of multimodal data in CSCL environments to support both individual and collective learning processes, with broader implications  for designing educational technologies that prepare students for the realities of clinical practice.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Learning Under Stress: Enhancing Team-Based Simulation Training with Multimodal Data. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Co-Design a Logic Model for Inclusive AI-Powered Learning
papers.authors: Ariel Han, Seth Corrigan, Shenshen Han, Kylie Peppler
papers.abstract: This study explores the development of a logic model to guide the design and implementation of an AI -powered story- authoring platform tailored for young learners, particularly those facing literacy challenges, such as English language learners, students wi th disabilities (e.g., dyslexia), and people with low socioeconomic status (SES). Amidst the rise of Generative AI tools, there's a need to bridge the gap between AI advancements and their practical use in K -12 educational settings. To address this, the researchers collaborated with primary school teachers, and synthesized insights from the literacy education literature. We conducted a co- design process, involving six educators, to identify the platform's potential users, features, functionalities, and desired outcomes. The findings emphasized the importance of making writing more accessible, with a focus on engaging students and motivating them to write. The proposed logic model underscores strategies like gamified elements, culturally - responsive imagery, and AI-generated mentor texts tailored to individual student needs.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Co-Design a Logic Model for Inclusive AI-Powered Learning. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Stepping Outside the Ivory Tower: How Can We Implement Multimodal Learning Analytics in Ecological Settings, and Turn Complex Temporal Data Sources into Actionable Insights?
papers.authors: Bertrand Schneider, Richard Davis, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Gautam Biswas, Marcelo Worsley, Nikol Rummel
papers.abstract: The field of Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is expanding, allowing researchers to capture rich, fine- grained data on learning processes in a variety of learning environments. High- quality process data can open the door for new insights on how people learn, creative interventions to support them, and build the foundation for personalized learning platforms. There is, however, a growing recognition that there is a lack of ecological implementations in MMLA (Cukurova, Giannakos & Martinez -Maldonado, 2020): the vast majority of projects are lab -based, which limit the generalizability and impact of multimodal sensing in education. This symposium brings together researchers who have used MMLA
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Stepping Outside the Ivory Tower: How Can We Implement Multimodal Learning Analytics in Ecological Settings, and Turn Complex Temporal Data Sources into Actionable Insights?. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Multimodal Observations of Pair Programming Processes
papers.authors: KU Leuven
papers.abstract: Previous research has identified promising avenues for investigating collaborative processes of pair  programming, a type of computer -supported collaborative learning. In our current research, we aim to advance our comprehension of the se dynamics, specifically within a shared visual workspace. To achieve this, we utilize multimodal learning analytics, emphasizing the integration of verbal  data and eye-tracking data, to provide more profound insights into this collaborative programming environment.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Multimodal Observations of Pair Programming Processes in a Shared Visual Workspace. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Investigating the Knowledge Building Process of Collaborative Learning between Student and Virtual Tutor Supported by ChatGPT
papers.authors: Xiaoyan Chu, Jiaqi Xu, Xuesong Zhai
papers.abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) such as ChatGPT has brought forth new possibilities in education, leading to further advancements in the design and application of virtual tutors. This study examine d the impact of collaborative learning with ChatGPT virtual tutors on academic performance among 94 graduate students. Utilizing the Tech-SEDA framework, discourse analysis was conducted on 344 dialogue data entries. Results indicate that while learners eng age in knowledge building with generative AI involving real- world tasks, the predominant mode of collaboration remains focused on information acquisition.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Tutor Supported by ChatGPT: A Discourse Analysis Learning between Student and Virtual. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Toward a Learning Agreement for Generative AI Use: First-Year
papers.authors: Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Ishari Amarasinghe, Davinia Hernández-Leo
papers.abstract: Tensions surrounding Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) use in university learning calls for a process bringing teachers and students together to define acceptable uses of AI in education. This article introduces first year student opinions on GenAI use and learning agreements as a flexible, participatory tool to govern its use. Results show inequality in students’ familiarity with GenAI, requests to be able to opt out of its use, and strong support for learning agreements as an instrument helping them learn to properly use AI and preventing them from being unfairly disadvantaged.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Toward a Learning Agreement for Generative AI Use: First-Year University Student Perspectives Marc Beardsley. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Evaluating a New Knowledge Building Analytics Tool (KBAT) Calixto Gutiérrez-Braojos KB (Zhu & Kim
papers.authors: Yang et al., reading of other notes, member relationships, discursive movements, discourse leadership, conceptual progress over time, promising ideas, conducted self - assessments, and technological, based on Authors
papers.abstract: The study explores the appraisal students make of the visualization tool K nowledge Building Analytics Tool (KBAT) to facilitate reflective self -assessments in Knowledge Building communities supported by the Knowledge Forum . This study carries out a design- based research methodology. Data collection involved a survey evaluating students’ perceptions of KBAT’s value. The study involved 122 students from an educational research course at the University of Granada, Spain. The results show that KBAT is highly valued by students. Inrtoduction Learning analytics is an emerging field with tremendous promise in enhancing educational processes . One of the educational theories that is addressing the challenge of developing Analytics tools is Knowledge Building, KB (Zhu & Kim, 2017 ). Th is educational theory  aims to empower students to collaborate in improving ideas (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2021). The KB pedagogy proposes that teachers should gradually entrust students with responsibilities linked to knowledge construction.  The teacher should create an educational environment that encourages students to share, question, and refine ideas about authentic problems . Students need to engage in knowledge improvement, which involves reflecting on the extent to which ideas are progressing and which issues should be addressed to continue deepening their understanding. Many recent studies affirm that conducting concurrent and reflective assessment sessions helps coordinate individual efforts to enhance shared knowledge (e.g., Yang et al., 2022).  KB is often implemented in  educational hybrid environment supported by technology named KF. This educational platform offers features that help students collaborate and enhance their knowledge, such as knowledge building scaffolds, (…), ideas promising tool. Over the past decade, researchers and educators have worked together to develop associated analytics  tool and visualization  for the Knowledge Forum. The progress made in the field of KB analytics tools is praiseworthy for its the innovative value it brings to the field of education. KB Analytics are still at a stage of development (see Zhu & Kim, 2017). This study builds upon funded research with the purpose of constructing and evaluate the Knowledge Building Analytics Tool (KBAT) . Our objective is to explore students' perceptions of the practical use of the KBAT and discuss how these perceptions can guide the improvement of future versions of the software.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Evaluating a New Knowledge Building Analytics Tool (KBAT) Calixto Gutiérrez-Braojos KB (Zhu & Kim. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Use of AI to Foster Greater Awareness and Reflexivity around Harmful Content in Online Discussion Tools
papers.authors: Kim MacKinnon, Jingyu Liu, Cresencia Fong, Jai Pandey
papers.abstract: In this project, we explore the development of an AI -powered harmful content detector for an online discussion tool. We explored three possible large language processors (Moderation API, roBERTa, and ChatGPT) using a dataset of 5,747 publicly- accessible online posts. Results indicated that the pre -trained, fine -tuned roBERTa processor was the most accurate at detecting harmful content and distinguishing it from non-harmful content. Context and theoretical perspective This study examined the development of an automated content moderation tool, particularly aimed at flagging posts containing harmful content within a locally developed online discussion platform. The larger aims of the project focus on the responsibility among K -12 schools to foster future -ready knowledge and skills among students (CMEC, 2016; OECD, 2018), such as effective communication and collaboration, and more recently AI- related global competencies (Dede, Etemadi, & Forshaw, 2021). Leveraging AI to reduce harm in online discussion Beginning in May 2023, we had an opportunity to leverage AI in the design of a school-based threaded discussion tool that would offer students the chance to engage in ‘sober second thought’ before posting a message that is potentially harmful. Liu (2023) notes there are limited open source options of generative AI language models to detect harmful online posts, though, there are some content detection models that target specific types of harmful content, such as hate speech (Abro et. al, 2020), and cyberbullying (Reynolds et. al, 2011). However, one classifier known as the Moderation API by OpenAI provided one potential opportunity to move towards a more expansive model, allowing for flagging of: hate, harassment, explicit sexual references, violence, and self -harm. Our rationale for integrating automated content detection into our school online discussion platform was threefold: 1) a fiduciary responsibility to ensure the safety of the learning environment (including online) for students, 2) the impracticality of manual daily monitoring of thousands of individual posts for potentially harmful content, and 3) student use of unfamiliar slang, shorthand, and insider references, which are continuously evolving. Furthermore, our intent was not simply to delete posts, or e ven to “reduce” (Gillespie, 2022) the noticeability of problematic posts, but to provide an opportunity for teachers to intervene to help foster development of important future-ready competencies, in this case digital rights and responsibilities. We added some basic features to the discussion interface that would allow for flagging of potentially harmful content including: 1) a warning message that appears to the student prior to posting if the AI processor has detected harmful content, and includes the option to ‘edit’ or ‘post’ anyway, 2) the ability for teachers to quickly see posts that have been flagged (either manually or by the AI) as having harmful content, 3) the ability for other students to manually and anonymously flag a post as harmful, and include a written rationale that would be seen by the teacher, and 4) the ability for the teacher to see a version history of a post (including deletions). Research question Our specific question was: Which of three large language processors were most effective at supporting accuracy, precision and recall of harmful content?
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Use of AI to Foster Greater Awareness and Reflexivity around Harmful Content in Online Discussion Tools. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Susan Harrington, Sonja Klein, Alice Catherine Fratoni, Charlott Sellberg, Oskar Lindwall
papers.abstract: Simulators have become central in professional training, in this case maritime education, where they support the development and assessment of skills and competencies required of competent seafarers. This study aims to inform the design of a learning analytics dashboard utilizing multimodal learning analytics to deliver automated, adaptive feedback to maritime students. Feedback is critical in simulator-based training, yet the characteristics of meaningful automated feedback in professional training remain underexplored. Drawing on a participatory design workshop with maritime students, the study examines tensions arising from the conceptualization of automated feedback. Using cultural historical activity theory, we frame tensions as opportunities for innovation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between students, instructors, and technology. In doing so, we offer insights into designing meaningful automated feedback for simulation training, and the need to balance students’ dual roles as learners and future professionals, reconciling collaborative learning with personalized feedback, and prioritizing educational goals over technological innovation.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Using Generative AI for Analyzing Student Reflections on Collaborative Virtual
papers.authors: Reality Creation, Shan Tang, Karen Yip, Carol K. K. Chan, Xiao Hu
papers.abstract: This study designed and examined an approach using ChatGPT for automatic coding of students’ reflection data in a Virtual Reality (VR) collaborative maker activity. We developed a coding scheme focusing on social-collaborative interactions and used few-shot prompting strategies for ChatGPT automatic coding. The results showed strong correspondence between ChatGPT and human coding on all eight codes (Kappa from 0.81 to 0.90), but variations exist on the overall performance of Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) for different codes based on F1 scores. Different explanations are proposed including clear definition of the codes and number of responses in different coding categories. The study contributed to illuminating processes underlying collaborative learning in maker activities, demonstrated the promise of GAI for automatic coding, and suggested implications for research and practice.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Using Generative AI for Analyzing Student Reflections on Collaborative Virtual Reality Creation. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Generative AI-Supported Collaboration in Interdisciplinary
papers.authors: Research Practice, Shotaro Naganuma, Tsubasa Minematsu, Kana Matsueda, Jun Oshima
papers.abstract: We report an empirical study of a three-day workshop on interdisciplinary research practice by 14 doctoral students supported by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to investigate how they use GenAI for their knowledge-building. They formed five teams and conducted presentations on promising interdisciplinary research proposals. Two high- performing teams’ discourses were analyzed in detail using a mixed-methods approach. We found that 1) students assigned four roles to GenAI (e.g., theme generation), 2) the frequency of students’ GenAI use was considerably limited, and 3) while GenAI use was limited to the initial theme establishment phase, students engaged in idea improvement by effectively integrating GenAI’s ideas. These findings suggest that the most difficult part of interdisciplinary collaboration for doctoral students is setting boundary objects in the initial phase, where GenAI can well-function. This study demonstrated that knowledge creators, such as doctoral students, can effectively collaborate using GenAI to create quality interdisciplinary collaborative research proposals.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Generative AI-Supported Collaboration in Interdisciplinary Research Practice. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Are You Seeing What I Am Talking About? Joint Attention Instruction for Collaborative Learners
papers.authors: William Pfannenstiel, Albulene Grajcevci, Andreas Korbach, Armin Weinberger, Universität des Saarlandes
papers.abstract: Joint attention is a crucial element in collaborative learning, often facilitated by group awareness tools highlighting the partner’s visual focus. Little is known, however, to what extent joint attention can also be differentially instructed guiding shared and mutual gaze. To determine if joint attention can be effectively instructed for, we conducted a 2×2 experimental laboratory study with the factors shared gaze instruction (with versus without) and dyadic gaze instruction (with versus without), consisting of 47 dyads (n = 94). Participants discussed the impact of social media use supported with a concept map on a digital whiteboard. We built on a multi-modal learning analytics framework to analyze participants’ behavioral responses via EDA and gaze tracking measurements. The results revealed that instructing for dyadic gaze reduces shared attention. Furthermore, there are differential correlations between shared moments of arousal and joint attention. Overall, joint attention instruction can guide learners’ focus in CSCL settings.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Are You Seeing What I Am Talking About? Joint Attention. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Reflective AI-Partnerships: How Middle Schoolers Balance Creativity and AI Collaboration
papers.authors: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Ariel Han, Andrew Rich, Shenshen Han, Kylie Peppler
papers.abstract: This study explores how middle school students navigate collaboration with generative AI in storytelling, focusing on their ability to balance AI contributions with their creative agency. Conducted during a workshop with Story AI, an interactive narrative-writing platform, this research involved participants aged 6 to 12 years from a predominantly Latinx community. Data from surveys, interviews, and writing outputs reveal that students engaged in reflective practices and demonstrated an emerging ability to critically modulate AI contributions. These findings engage with recent CSCL studies, including Cress and Kimmerle’s (2023) insights into knowledge transformation and Borge et al.’s (2024) exploration of metacognitive reflection, by situating co-writing as a dynamic context for fostering collaboration and agency. Implications include designing learning environments that explicitly scaffold student reflection on AI collaboration as an essential skill for navigating human-AI partnerships. This research highlights co-writing as a valuable avenue for advancing reflective and creative thinking in educational settings.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Reflective AI-Partnerships: How Middle Schoolers Balance Creativity and AI Collaboration. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Processes Matter: How ML/GAI Approaches Could Support Open Qualitative Coding of Online Discourse Datasets
papers.authors: John Chen, Alexandros Lotsos, Grace Wang, Lexie Zhao, Bruce Sherin, Uri Wilensky, Michael Horn
papers.abstract: Open coding, a key inductive step in qualitative research, discovers and constructs concepts from human datasets. However, capturing extensive and nuanced aspects or “coding moments” can be challenging, especially with large discourse datasets. While some studies explore machine learning (ML)/Generative AI (GAI)'s potential for open coding, few evaluation studies exist. We compare open coding results by five recently published ML/GAI approaches and four human coders, using a dataset of online chat messages around a mobile learning software. Our systematic analysis reveals ML/GAI approaches' strengths and weaknesses, uncovering the complementary potential between humans and AI. Line-by-line AI approaches effectively identify content-based codes, while humans excel in interpreting conversational dynamics. We discussed how embedded analytical processes could shape the results of ML/GAI approaches. Instead of replacing humans in open coding, researchers should integrate AI with and according to their analytical processes, e.g., as parallel co-coders.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Processes Matter: How ML/GAI Approaches Could Support Open Qualitative Coding of Online Discourse Datasets. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Mirroring What’s in the Shared Repertoires of Two Communities of Practice: A Cultural-Historical Perspective Using Generative AI
papers.authors: Thérèse Laferrière, Université Laval, Elizabeth S. Charles
papers.abstract: This paper explores the development of the shared repertoires (Wenger, 1998) of two web-supported Communities of Practice (CoPs). The co-authors of this paper were the initiators of these CoPs and continue to be involved in them. Using the shared repertoire of each of these communities as a lens, the evolution of their activity was explored. Referring to the CHAT’s change lab process of mirroring to participants their past activity (Engeström, 1987, 2015), two generative AI tools were prompted to focus on the websites of the two CoPs, especially collaborative activities and artefacts, and to ‘report on’ the evolution of their shared repertoires. Accounts underwent human validation. For ethical reasons, no transcript was analysed of the interactions between the participants that may have led, through meaning negotiation, to the production or use of artefacts as well as to problem setting, problem solving or knowledge building. Results show that 1) the generative AI tools were accurate in their ‘reports’; and 2) identified possible limitations in the shared repertoires; such observations providing topics for future negotiation of values among members and between these communities.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Mirroring What’s in the Shared Repertoires of Two Communities of Practice: A Cultural-Historical Perspective Using Generative AI. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Interaction Analysis between Generative AI and High School Students in Scientific Projects
papers.authors: Students in Scientific Projects, Ayano Ohsaki
papers.abstract: This study investigates interaction patterns between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and high school students as they develop science research projects. Specifically, it examines GenAI’s behavior, focusing on interaction patterns and response appropriateness. The analysis indicates that GenAI frequently provides unsolicited advice and generates responses eight times longer than student inputs despite predefined constraints. This study proposes a visualization method for the interaction imbalance between learners and GenAI, providing valuable insight into the relationship between interaction balance and learning in future computer-supported collaborative learning research.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Interaction Analysis between Generative AI and High School Students in Scientific Projects. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Design and Play in Real Time: A Participatory Design Approach for Autistic Children to Design Online Play with Peers
papers.authors: Yiqi Xiao, Jiabei Xu
papers.abstract: This paper presents a participatory design approach for children, designers, and educators to collaboratively create inclusive digital play environments that foster interactions between neurodiverse and neurotypical children. Integrating generative AI (GenAI) empowers children to actively contribute to game design while engaging in the play with their peers without adult mediation, highlighting the potential of such methods to foster inclusive collaboration among children, between children and adults, and between children and technology. A Call for creating inclusive social opportunities online Like other children, autistic children often desire peer friendships (Rodda & Estes, 2018) yet frequently face social challenges (Lord & Magill-Evans, 1995). These include difficulties with language, sensory processing, and interpreting social cues—such as jokes, eye contact, or facial expressions (Ghanouni et al., 2019; Aherne, 2023)— which can lead to reduced or atypical peer interactions. Given these challenges in face-to-face communication, online spaces offer alternative avenues for social expression. Research shows a strong preference among autistic children for screen-based media, especially video games (Mazurek & Engelhardt, 2013). As Barrington Campbell, an autistic adult, shared: “If you are autistic, this can feel more than stressful... Online gaming means autistic people can play in an environment we feel comfortable in and can control” (National Autistic Society, 2024). However, autistic children also face heightened online safety risks compared to peers (Macmillan et al., 2020). Mainstream digital spaces rarely support neurodiverse communication and often neglect their well-being in interactions with non-autistic users. Few games, whether commercial or academic, are designed to connect autistic and neurotypical children through shared interests in gameplay (Spiel & Gerling, 2021; Xiao, 2024). The research team that designed Zopy, a collaborative iPad game that successfully fostered friendship among autistic students without adult mediation, encouraged designers to create more games that reflect the diverse spectrum of social behaviors in peer collaboration (Boyd et al., 2015). Building on this, more design approaches are needed to guide the development of such inclusive applications. This paper proposes a participatory approach to digital play, involving collaboration among children, educators, designers, and GenAI. The rationale and methods for each type of collaboration are illustrated through the design case Together Tales, a collaborative storybook making game (Xiao, 2024). Collaboration among children, educators, and designers Why involve children? Traditionally, adults have controlled all aspects of the design process, even when the intended users are children. As Druin (2002) noted, children have distinct preferences, curiosities, and needs that differ from those of adults. Their input is therefore essential for designing effective products. Involving children not only improves outcomes but also ensures they feel valued and heard. Despite growing recognition of children as design partners, research involving autistic children remains limited. Most games for this group adopt top-down approaches with educational or medical goals, often overlooking their interests (Spiel & Gerling, 2021). Given the social challenges autistic children face, it is vital to include them in designing social games tailored to their needs. It is also worth noting that autistic children, like other neurodiverse groups, may be natural design partners. They often exhibit traits commonly labeled as “gifted,” such as excelling in creativity, visual-spatial skills, and attention to detail (Armstrong, 2010), making them highly capable contributors to design processes. How to involve children? In many participatory design (PD) practices, researchers acknowledge that children often struggle with verbal communication, particularly when dealing with abstract concepts (Druin, 2002). This issue is likely to be even more pronounced in collaborations between autistic children and adults. As a result, drawing is frequently used as an alternative form of contribution to the design process (Hunt et al., 2023). In the approach proposed here, children express ideas through drawings and then select AI-generated elements that match their vision. These are directly incorporated into the final design. The technical implementation of this GenAI collaboration is discussed in later sections. In Together Tales, children are prompted by animations within the game to draw characters they imagine appearing in specific story scenarios. They then select the generated images that best match their vision. The selected images retain certain features and are integrated into the subsequent storylines, influencing the progression of the narrative. Why involve educators? It is a common practice to involve educators in the participatory design process involving children (Piedade et al., 2024; Ey & Spears, 2020), to leverage their expertise and insights, which help ensure pedagogical guidance. In the context of this paper, educators primarily function as stakeholders, providing critical insights that bridge pedagogical goals with the needs and interests of the children. How to involve educators? While understanding why educators should be involved is relatively straightforward, addressing how to involve them effectively requires deeper consideration. Excessive involvement by educators may reduce the freedom and space for children to contribute, while insufficient involvement risks a lack of critical information in the design. How can we achieve an appropriate level of participation? The participatory design process proposed in this paper borrows from the concept of guided play (Weisberg et al., 2016). It highlights the strategy that adults create a setting that emphasizes a specific learning goal while still allowing children the freedom to explore and interact within the environment independently. Research shows that compared to a free setting and a highly structured setting, children’s active participation in discovery, combined with appropriate scaffolding from a knowledgeable adult, a higher level of engagement and better learning result (Sim & Xu, 2015). In Together Tales (Fig. 1), educators define the overarching storyline—the goal of the journey for two players, structure of activities in which children engage during digital play. These activities may include collaborative drawing, assembling puzzle pieces, organizing photos to reconstruct a story, or other creative tasks. While the framework provides guidance, the specifics—such as what to draw, the themes of the photos, or the approach to completing the activity—are shaped by the children’s prior choices and left open for their exploration. This balance between structure and freedom ensures meaningful engagement and allows children to take ownership of their creative process. Figure 1 A Demonstration of The Mechanism of Together Tales. The role of designers/researchers Rather than focusing solely on the final product, designers and researchers should prioritize creating innovative processes and frameworks that position users and stakeholders as active, independent contributors. They are also responsible for assessing the technical feasibility of stakeholders’ ideas to ensure the process runs smoothly. Collaboration between autistic and neurotypical children Why involve both groups? Peers support autistic children’s play in ways adults cannot (Jones, 1991), yet few digital play environments reflect neurodiverse interests. Many games focus narrowly on autistic children’s social challenges rather than fostering inclusive or neurodivergent-centered experiences (Spiel & Gerling, 2021; Xiao, 2024). Two major misconceptions contribute to this gap. The first is that only autistic children benefit from peer interaction. Jones (1991) identified self-disclosure, trust, and companionship as key to friendship satisfaction. A global study of 2,555 autism experts emphasized traits like morality, trustworthiness, and kindness in autistic individuals (de Schipper et al., 2016)—qualities that make them valuable friends. Without opportunities to engage, neurotypical children may miss out on meaningful relationships, thus they too need to learn how to interact and collaborate with autistic peers. The second misconception is that autistic children are not capable of forming strong friendships. Though their styles may differ, research increasingly shows that autistic children build meaningful relationships with both neurotypical and autistic peers (Rodda & Estes, 2018). Therefore, creating more opportunities for positive interaction is essential to support relationship-building between neurodiverse children. How to involve both groups? Collaborative play—where players coordinate actions toward a shared goal—effectively fosters social interaction between autistic and neurotypical children (Reuter et al., 2014; Khatab et al., 2024). Moreover, Piedade et al. (2024) found that creating such artifacts enhances self-determination in autistic children. While few studies compare artifact co-design to digital collaboration within the screen in terms of social outcomes, the approach of “collaborative making through game” shows strong potential and merits further exploration. In Together Tales, children collaborate on playful design decisions, such as choosing what kind of backpack to include, determining the type of animal characters they encounter, and deciding the sequence of photos displayed on a wall. These decisions collectively weave a unique narrative. At the end of the game, children receive a co-authored, printable digital storybook as a tangible artifact of their collaboration. Collaboration between children and GenAI Why involve GenAI? The development of AI technology has significantly transformed and advanced educational practices. For example, AI can assist teachers in designing and delivering personalized, timely, iterative, and enriching learning experiences (Nguyen, 2023). However, a significant portion of current methodologies view AI as an extension of roles traditionally held by educators, behavior analysts, or other adult experts, aiming to achieve previously unattainable efficiencies (Amiri et al., 2017; Shahamiri & Thabtah, 2020). Few approaches aim to help children enhance their own abilities, limiting their opportunities to participate meaningfully in the design process and reducing their agency within support systems. Moreover, while discussions have highlighted the potential of AI as a creative assistant in participatory design (Zhao, 2024), research focusing on its application for children— especially autistic children—is scarce. Despite this, AI has been used in various contexts to support youth in creating original work outside the PD framework. Ali et al. (2021) demonstrated how GenAI supported K-12 students and educators in co-designing learning materials, boosting teacher confidence. Such cases underscore AI’s potential to enhance children’s creativity and support its further exploration in participatory design with autistic children. Figure 2 Character Creation to Collaborative Storytelling in Together Tales. How to involve GenAI? Through the versatile application of GenAI, generative image model (GIM) empowers children to transform their sketches into content-consistent images. Vision-language model (VLM) further enhances this process by converting visual outputs into descriptive text, integrating these capabilities with large language model (LLM) and carefully crafted prompts, AI can generate adaptive visual content tailored to children’s preferences, all while maintaining alignment with educator-defined scaffolds to ensure meaningful engagement. In Together Tales, generative AI is implemented using ComfyUI combined with Stable Diffusion and ChatGPT APIs (Fig. 2). Summary This paper presents an innovative design process through Together Tales—a storybook game designed to foster collaboration between autistic and non-autistic children. The process unfolds across three levels of collaboration. First, among children, collaborative making fosters neurodiverse peer-to-peer interactions, cultivating authentic and inclusive social connections. Second, between children and educators, the approach ensures that pedagogical goals are met while providing children with the freedom to create and collaborate independently, striking a thoughtful balance between guidance and autonomy. Third, between children and generative AI technologies, the integration of GenAI showcases AI’s potential to enhance their creative agency and further enables them to co- create unique experiences and products for themselves with adults and their peers. Discussion This participatory design model holds great potential for broader application—not only for autistic children but also for those with ADHD, dyslexia, and other neurodiverse profiles, in collaboration with neurotypical peers. The educational principles underpinning this design, such as collaborative play and scaffolding, are rooted in general education practices, suggesting their adaptability across various neurotypes and learning contexts. While this approach emphasizes children’s contributions to one aspect of game design, future work will explore AI integration across the full design process, building toward a more comprehensive child-centered framework. Upcoming iterations will also include structured observations and post-play interviews to assess its effectiveness. References Aherne, D. (2023). The pocket guide to neurodiversity. Frontiers in Communication, 9. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1440384 Using Markov Chain Analysis to Study the Relations Between Emotions, Cognitive Actions, and Performance in Collaborative Learning Ashwin T S, Vanderbilt University, ashwindixit9@gmail.com Caitlin Snyder, University of Detroit Mercy, snydercr@udmercy.edu Srigowri Mayasandra Prasanna, Vanderbilt University, srigowri.mayasandra.prasanna@vanderbilt.edu Naveeduddin Mohammed, Vanderbilt University, naveeduddin.mohammed@vanderbilt.edu Gautam Biswas, Vanderbilt University, gautam.biswas@vanderbilt.edu Abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in STEM+C education involves cognitive coordination and emotional regulation during joint tasks. Prior research has examined discrete affective states in learning environments but less is known about how these emotions evolve over time and affect CPS behavior. This study investigates the temporal dynamics of five emotions—engagement, confusion, boredom, delight, and frustration—using Markov Chain analysis of data from high school pairs building computational models in the C2STEM environment. Emotional transitions aligned with cognitive processes, seen in interaction patterns like PLAY, ADJUST, and BUILD, to analyze affect during modeling. Results show that emotional trajectories closely relate to cognitive actions, including construction, simulation testing, and debugging. Transitions that maintained engagement linked to productive collaboration and stronger performance, while ongoing frustration and boredom indicated disengagement progress.

papers.title: Generative AI in Project-Based Learning for Sustainable Development
papers.authors: Davinia Hernández-Leo, Emily Theophilou, Shatha N. Alkhasawneh
papers.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) offers potential to enhance learning scenarios. However, research on specific use-cases and roles within educational frameworks is limited. This paper focuses on UNESCO’s Education for Sustainable Development framework and its recommendation to use Project-Based Learning (PBL) to develop key-competences for addressing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The research investigates expert teachers' views on the potential for human-AI collaboration, focusing on the role of genAI in use-cases designed to enhance individual and collaborative learning within PBLxSDG. A workshop involving 33 participants yielded 11 use-cases. Along with 10 use-cases derived from the literature and evaluations from participants, forming the foundation of our analysis. Insights from our analysis saw genAI assuming diverse roles for human-AI collaboration within PBLxSDG. However, concerns were raised about overreliance on AI, learning outcomes, and the need for teacher guidance. This work provides insights for educators and researchers exploring genAI implementation in collaborative, active learning scenarios.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Generative AI in Project-Based Learning for Sustainable Development Davinia Hernández-Leo. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Towards Actionable Collaborative Discourse Analysis: Bridging Advanced Computational Analysis with Practical Implementation
papers.authors: Yeonji Jung, Xinran Zhu, Jun Oshima, Bodong Chen, Jewoong Moon, Laura McNeill, Christopher Edmonds, Kazem Banihashem, Omid Noroozi, Indrani Dey, Sadhana Puntambekar, Tiereney Janya Jackson
papers.abstract: Since the inception of learning analytics, the CSCL community has been applying a range of methods to examine collaborative discourse, such as natural language processing and networked approaches. Despite significant advancements in methods, a critical gap persists in translating these data-driven insights into actionable strategies to inform pedagogical decisions. The proposed hybrid symposium seeks to bridge this gap by engaging learning scientists, CSCL researchers, and educators in discussions that integrate advanced discourse analytics with pedagogical design. Through five diverse presentations, the symposium will explore the integration of advanced discourse analysis techniques, such as networked approaches, multimodal analytics, and clustering analysis, into pedagogically meaningful designs and actionable pedagogical insights for collaborative learning environments. By fostering dialogue on the challenges and opportunities in contextualizing computational insights, this symposium aims to establish actionable approaches for enriching collaborative discourse and advancing the broader CSCL community’s theoretical, methodological, and practical understanding.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Analysis with Practical Implementation Advanced Computational. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Enhancing Peer Feedback Practices with Generative AI
papers.authors: Martin Greisel, Omid Noroozi, Golnoush Haddadian, Xingshi Gao, Maryam Alqassab, Kazem Banihashem, Hassan Khosravi, Stanislav Pozdniakov, Christian D. Schunn, Qiuchen Yu, Nikol Rummel
papers.abstract: Providing peer feedback is a powerful learning activity. However, its potential is not always realized. To improve feedback provision and uptake, AI can augment peer feedback provision and reception processes. However, little is known about how students use AI in the context of peer feedback, what aspects of AI feedback are associated with higher quality of human peer feedback, and how AI feedback can be implemented as part of the instructional design to best facilitate learning. In addition, research needs to find ways to harness the power of AI while minimizing its high resource requirements. This symposium will answer these questions and provide insights into the latest developments in using AI in peer feedback research. Generative AI as a potential solution to challenges inherent to peer feedback Providing feedback is essential for enhancing student learning and performance (Hattie & Timperley, 2007). However, due to heavy workloads, time constraints, and large class sizes, teachers often face challenges in providing feedback. Peer feedback is increasingly regarded as a valuable alternative to teacher feedback (Valero Haro et al., 2023). By actively involving students in the feedback exchange process to critically evaluate their peers’ written work, peer feedback not only helps reduce teacher workload but also greatly enhances their learning by activating deep learning processes such as comparing, evaluating, reflecting, and critical reasoning (Kollar & Fischer, 2010; Noroozi et al., 2023). Meta-analyses confirm this learning advantage (Double et al., 2020). Despite these benefits, students often have problems regarding how to provide high-quality feedback and how to use feedback from their peers to improve their performance. Providing high-quality feedback is a complex task that requires considerable cognitive processing to meticulously evaluate peers’ assignments, identify problems, and propose constructive remedies (Banihashem et al., 2024). Consequently, though these complex cognitive processes are key to the undoubted general efficacy of peer feedback, it is not surprising that this feedback often is not of sufficient quality, for example, lacking relevant criticism (Patchan et al., 2013). In terms of feedback reception and uptake, challenges arise from psychological, emotional, and social barriers, including students’ perceptions of their peers and the feedback they receive, concerns about trustworthiness, and varying levels of tolerance for receiving and accepting critical feedback (Kerman et al., 2024). These challenges can hinder the potential impact of peer feedback and ultimately affect learning outcomes in a negative way. Thus, effective interventions are needed to address these challenges. Traditionally, scaffolding has been used to improve the quality of feedback (Hornstein et al., in press). For example, sentence starters guide students to focus their feedback on the most relevant aspects of a task solution. However, such scaffolds are typically not adaptive and thus squander further learning (Sharma et al., 2024). In contrast, generative artificial intelligence (AI) can efficiently analyze written task solutions and produce tailored, individualized feedback (Escalante et al., 2023). Unlike human teachers, generative AI is not overwhelmed by the large amount of text that students typically produce in a peer feedback environment. Instead, AI can use this rich textual data to deliver interventions that are tailored to the individual needs of each student. However, educators need to be careful that AI does not replace learning activities such as providing feedback, thereby eliminating learning opportunities. It is therefore important to find ways of combining AI and peer feedback so that AI enhances (rather than undermines) learning. Different ways of how to integrate generative AI into peer feedback This symposium brings together four empirical papers from different parts of the world (Netherlands, Australia, Germany, USA) that explore how generative AI can address these challenges and improve peer feedback practices in educational settings. Specifically, the papers explore how AI can support the feedback process by improving the quality of feedback provided, fostering deeper cognitive engagement, and scaling feedback activities in ways not previously possible. Paper 1 from Noroozi, Haddadian, Gao, Schunn, Alqassab, and Banihashem investigates how many students use generative AI, which AI system specifically they use, and how this use relates to the resulting peer feedback features and the uptake of peer feedback comments. In doing so, the study acknowledges that AI is already part of students’ regular learning practices and promotes its competent use by providing instructional support on effectively prompting large language models. Paper 2 from Khosravi, Pozdniakov, and Noroozi goes a step further and includes generative AI into the instructional design so that it is readily available to all students. This integration enables the use of the log data that students produce while interacting with the system. This allows the authors to analyze not only the human peer feedback features, but also the AI-generated feedback and how students interact with it. Paper 3 from Greisel, Hornstein, and Kollar compares the effects of two different ways of delivering AI feedback. On the one hand, the AI provides feedback on the peers’ initial solutions available to the peer reviewers while generating their own feedback. On the other hand, AI provides feedback on the peer reviewers’ feedback message. Using a randomized controlled experimental design, the authors show that augmenting human with AI feedback does not necessarily surpass traditional peer feedback. However, AI seems to be able to compete with human peer feedback though replacing the feedback providing process. Paper 4 from Schunn and Yu emphasizes efficiency, as the use of large language models is resource- intensive. It describes how to identify feedback quality indicators that can then be applied to peer feedback data without the high cost of LLMs, thus solving both the problem of how to afford to apply LLMs to very large datasets, and how to avoid ethical and privacy concerns. In addition, Paper 4 also demonstrates that AI can help researchers distinguish effective from ineffective instructional scaffolds without having to conduct extensive intervention studies. In this study, the authors use AI to analyze the instructions themselves, rather than student responses. As a result, instructors can learn how to design their scaffolds to improve peer feedback quality. To summarize, the central question of this symposium examines the extent to which AI-supported scaffolding can improve the effectiveness of peer feedback processes. Paper 1 showed that students already independently use AI to support their peer feedback process. However, this self-initiative is significantly correlated with low self-efficacy beliefs and is primarily limited to the provision of feedback. Paper 2’s hypothesis that optimized accessibility through full system integration leads to a significant increase in learning outcomes could not be confirmed in general terms. Rather, classical instructional design elements that influence learning motivation seemed to be decisive. This finding is supported by the results of Study 3, which showed no differential benefit of different AI implementations for students so far. Instead, Study 4 points to how instructionally relevant features can be identified by the help of AI to inform future instructional design and peer feedback scaffolds. Paper 1: Supporting peer feedback provision and uptake with genAI Omid Noroozi, Golnoush Haddadian, Xingshi Gao, Christian D. Schunn, Maryam Alqassab, Seyyed Kazem Banihashem

papers.title: Exploring GenAI Technologies within
papers.authors: Emma Anderson (Co-Chair), Grace C. Lin (Co-Chair), Amelia Farid, Mic Fenech, Brandon Hanks,
papers.abstract: Since the release of OpenAI ChatGPT along with other Large Language Models (LLMs), a surge of AI tools has been offered to teachers and students. Beyond LLMs’ common uses as efficiency tools and 1:1 tutors, we contend that AI advancements provide opportunities to support robust student learning in other approaches, specifically in collaborative learning groups. In this symposium, we present the ways in which generative AI can be used to facilitate jigsaw work, promote discussion, identify confusions and conflicts, and create new knowledge with student groups. Interactive demonstration of the tools is built into the symposium so together as a group, we can learn more about how to use Gen AI to facilitate and promote group learning. Objectives of the session The advancement in generative AI (genAI) technology in the past couple years has pushed education innovations, expanding possibilities to support student learning. Unfortunately, most use cases of the emerging technologies still center around decades old problems, for example, one-on-one tutoring and interactions. Much less is known in the underexplored space of genAI in collaborative learning. In this symposium, we seek to start the conversation investigating the state of the field when it comes to collaborative AI in the classroom. Particularly, what do people mean by collaborative AI within learning environments? Where and how are people exploring collaboration? How does AI fit into collaboration with humans in the classroom settings? Overview of the presentation The papers in this symposium cover a wide range of ways for supporting collaboration with AI in diverse learning environments. To answer our research questions, we present a range of approaches to collaborative AI starting with more conceptual and moving towards evidence-based papers. For example, paper 1 addresses RQ1 by presenting h ow generative AI and humans can jointly regulate collaborative learning in a new model, while paper 6 addresses it by showcasing promising evidence for genAI to provide support for human collaborative knowledge building. While all papers address RQ2 in different ways, we highlight paper 2 that involves LLM in jigsaw activities and paper 3 where genAI supports community norms and moderates discussion. For our last question, we spotlight papers 4 and 5 where researchers are exploring how students engage with conversational agents during group work. Scholarly significance Group work is inherently challenging. The “triple problem solving space” framework posits that group work involves cognitive, social, and affective components that requires real-time calibration (Nieswandt et al., 2020). Cognitive, task-related challenges can sometimes lead to interpersonal conflicts, especially when students’ social skills may still be developing, derailing the collaborative learning goals (Lee et al., 2015). Therefore, facilitating meaningful group work and ensuring all students have opportunities to participate can be difficult, and teachers often feel underprepared to address group work (Bennet et al., 2010). GenAI tools can potentially alleviate these problems. In a literature review of the roles of collaborative AI, Tan and colleagues (2022) identified four types of AI support for collaborative learning: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive. In these papers we reveal ways of going beyond these four categories. The symposium contributes to existing literature by exploring the breadth of ideas for supporting collaborative learning with AI. We dig into the dynamics and challenges of a group collaboration that varies based on the learning context, learning objectives, and learning design and ask how and how well GenAI can help address these concerns. Structure This face to face symposium will be organized as a structured poster session. Each presenter will begin with a brief elevator pitch (no more than one minute) to introduce their project. Presenters will then move to their respective stations, where participants can view posters, watch demonstrations, and engage in discussions. Remote presenters will provide video walkthroughs of their posters and be available on Zoom to answer questions from participants. Shared hybrid intelligent regulation of collaborative learning model Andy Nguyen The swift advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly with Generative AI (GenAI), have substantially impacted numerous sectors, reshaping both professional and educational environments (Giannakos, 2024). These shifts highlight an urgent need to reimagine and reform educational practices while also emphasizing the importance of reinforcing human skills, such as collaboration and self-regulation. Collaborative learning has long been recognized as a highly effective approach to cultivate these competencies and Socially Shared Regulation of Learning (SSRL) theory offers a useful framework to examine how learners co-regulate and manage their learning efforts in collaborative settings (Järvelä et al., 2023). Recent models, including Järvelä and Hadwin’s (2024) trigger framework and Singh and Muis’s (2024) integrated SSRL model, offer advanced insights into SSRL, enhancing our ability to support collaborative learning. While these models mark significant progress in SSRL research, they have yet incorporated the potential role of GenAI as an active partner in collaborative learning. GenAI differs from prior technologies through its capacity for human-like interactions across various modalities (Nguyen et al., 2024). Furthermore, with machine reinforcement learning, GenAI can have the ability to continuously improve based on human interactions (Counts et al., 2024). However, there remains an ongoing debate regarding the extent to which learners should develop skills that allow them to perform tasks independently of AI support (Giannakos, 2024; Nguyen, 2025). Given that technology such as GenAI is deeply embedded in modern society and workplaces, many tasks now rely on an interplay between human and technological capabilities. Socio-technical theory emphasizes that any organizational system’s effectiveness relies on an integrated view of both 'social' and 'technical' dimensions as interdependent parts of a complex system. Recently, the concept of hybrid intelligence has emerged, aiming to merge human and artificial intelligence in ways that yield outcomes unattainable by either entity alone (Nguyen et al., 2024; Nguyen, 2025). Within this hybrid intelligence paradigm, human-AI shared regulation is seen as vital (Järvelä et al., 2023; Nguyen, 2025). Taking a socio-technical system approach and building up from previous SSRL frameworks ( Järvelä et al., 2023; Järvelä & Hadwin, 2024; Singh & Muis, 2024), this study proposes the model for Shared Hybrid Intelligent Regulation of Collaborative Learning (SHIRCL) (as shown in Figure 1). Figure 1 Shared Hybrid Intelligent Regulation of Collaborative Learning (SHIRCL) Model The framework comprises both individual-level conditions and group-level dynamics in human–AI teaming for learning. At the individual level, human conditions include cognitive, affective, motivational, and metacognitive factors, while AI-related conditions refer to its technological affordances, learning capabilities, and underlying knowledge bases. At the group level, the framework conceptualizes AI as an active, adaptive entity that interacts dynamically with human learners through sensing, sense-making and adaptation. The collaboration is situated within defined task conditions, highlighting the interdependence between human and AI agents in joint learning activities as well as in understanding each other. The SHIRCL framework seeks to not only provide insights into the dynamics of SSRL in collaborative learning involving multiple learners and GenAI agents but also guide the design, development, and evaluation of learning tasks and GenAI agents that can effectively engage in shared regulation with human learners in collaborative learning contexts. Responsible innovation for AI partners in jigsaw classrooms Emily Doherty, Leanne Hirshfield The Jigsaw Classroom, first implemented in desegregated classrooms, was a pivotal innovation in educational techniques aimed at fostering collaborative learning and social unity (Perkins and Tagler 2011; Aronson 1978). The impact of the Jigsaw Classroom continues to make it a well-established and common collaborative technique in today’s classrooms. However, with increasingly more students in classrooms, it is often difficult for teachers to closely monitor many small group collaborations at once. This presents an opportunity to leverage the growing toolbox of Generative AI (GenAI) resources to support collaboration during jigsaw activities. One way to leverage GenAI tools to support small group collaboration is through conversational agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), due to their ability to understand human language and produce real- time, intelligent interventions. In this commentary, we build upon the empirical findings exploring the human- centered design and evaluation of an LLM-based jigsaw partner to support small group collaboration (Doherty et al., 2025). Fifty-eight groups of dyads and triads (145 participants), aged 12-17,collaborated in a jigsaw activity and were assigned to be assisted by our agent or not. The results showed decreased self-reported ratings of social loafing and increased use of language related to respectful collaboration in interactions with the agent compared to those without. Our studies demonstrate both the potential and the risks of integrating LLMs into collaborative learning settings: while they can scaffold group learning and encourage inclusive dialogue, they can also reinforce undesired social dynamics if not carefully designed. Thus, the use of LLMs as educational supports requires a responsible innovation approach (Stilgoe et al., 2013). Concerns around model selection, transparency, and limitations of out-of-the-box LLMs require careful attention (Williams et al., 2023). We advocate for a human-centered design process that incorporates educator and learner perspectives throughout development, prototyping, and iterative evaluation (Amershi et al., 2014, Wang et al., 2021). In this talk, we detail the opportunities, challenges, and implications of designing GenAI tools for collaborative learning. In particular, we focus on the importance of human-centered design and evaluation practices to ensure that such tools promote equity, lift underrepresented voices, and stay aligned with the original social goals of the Jigsaw Classroom. From learning about to figuring out: AI-partner embedded curricula for meaningful collaboration and understanding Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Peter Foltz We describe the development of an AI-partner embedded-curriculum unit, the AI-Games Unit, and the opportunities that it provides for middle school students to work collaboratively and figure out how AI systems work. We have iteratively developed and refined an AI partner that supports collaboration and a curricular unit that addresses how AI systems are used to moderate online communities. We argue that by 1) engaging students in a unit about moderation and 2) giving students a chance to experience and examine an AI moderation tool enables students to co-construct ideas about how AI can be used to foster equitable online communities. Incorporating AI partners integrated with curricula addresses the challenge of how to promote deep conceptual learning via rich socio-collaborative learning experiences for all students. While the benefits of collaborative learning are well-known, contemporary classrooms still face challenges in implementing collaborative learning experiences (D’Mello et al., 2024). Teachers face the challenge of orchestrating rich, collaborative experiences in their classroom (Chin, 2007). Students must also attend to the relational aspects of attending to and building off of one another’s ideas (Chowning et al., 2023). Our approach to supporting collaboration involves the development of an LLM-based AI partner that is meaningfully integrated into a curricular unit that addresses key ideas in the AI4K12 framework (AI4K12, 2024). The Community Builder (CoBI) AI Partner supports the relational dimension of collaboration. Students use CoBi to define a set of “community agreements” or norms of behavior (e.g., being equitable, respectful, and moving thinking forward). After this criteria is established, CoBi listens in on student talk to identify examples of these agreements during small group activity to identify how students are engaging in collaboration. Classrooms can review CoBi’s outputs and reflect on their joint collaboration and also discuss the strength, limitations and opportunities for improvement. Throughout CoBI, multiple AI-based approaches are incorporated to best characterize student collaboration. CoBi is used within a Storyline unit (Reiser et al., 2021) where students take the lead on working together to build an explanation of how AI systems are used to moderate online communities. CoBi is used at multiple points throughout the unit to support students in examining how AI- and human- moderation systems work. Our preliminary analysis of use in an 8th grade ELA classroom suggests that the AI-partner embedded unit creates a rich learning environment for engaging with AI systems in ways that provide students with opportunities to “look under the hood” and facilitate more meaningful collaborations. For example, a teacher reported that using CoBi supported students in generating ideas about specific prompts that reflected different dimensions of collaboration. Moreover, reflections on CoBi’s output also allowed students to engage in conversations about how different perspectives and design decisions underlying AI systems can lead to bias in its output. In this talk, we will demonstrate the integration of AI partners into curricula and discuss the novel opportunities for AI-embedded curricular units for supporting students in meaningful collaborative learning about AI systems. Designing chatbots to enrich discussions and promote systems thinking Ha Nguyen, Victoria Nguyen, Sara Ludovise, Rosella Santagata Objectives. We will describe the development process of different AI chatbots (using GPT-4 as the base) and their integration into collaborative learning in a high school environment science curriculum. We co-create five chatbots—demonstrating varied perspectives around climate change’s impact on a local marine ecosystem—with students, teachers, and environmental educators. The chatbots role-play as a fisherman, a college student, a social media influencer, a kelp researcher, and a civil engineer. Following the jigsaw method (Aronson, 1978), students in groups of four are given individual tasks to converse with different chatbots and collect information. Then, they share the information with groupmates to collectively refine their models of climate change’s root causes and causal relationships. Interactions with the chatbots prompt students to consider factors often overlooked in environmental education, including climate change's impacts over time and space and across communities. We ask: How are the chatbots developed to integrate community perspectives? How are they integrated into small- group discussions to facilitate systems understanding? Perspectives. In prior virtual learning environments, pedagogical agents often had limited, pre-defined dialogues. Leveraging the advances of Large Language Models (LLMs) to facilitate human-like dialogues, we design our chatbots to not just provide information, but also elicit students’ ideas, link to multifaceted data sources (e.g., scientific sources, personal stories), and deliver feedback on students’ models. To design the chatbots’ dialogues, we build on the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014), which positions interactive and constructive activities as the most conducive to learning, compared to active and passive engagement. The chatbots encourage students to explain their understanding (active), while building on students’ ideas (interactive).

papers.title: Collaborating with Generative AI for Learning?
papers.authors: Davinia Hernández-Leo, Omid Noroozi, Golnoush Haddadian, Kazem Banihashem
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, driven by large language models (LLMs), are increasingly explored for their potential in educational contexts. However, significant concerns remain regarding their efficacy, cognitive impacts, and ethical implications. The Computer Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community faces critical questions regarding the broader implications of this technology for the field. While GenAI offers advanced opportunities for collaborative learning through conversational interactions and other functions, research in this area is still in its early stages. This symposium presents five contributions that explore the opportunities, challenges, and initial findings of integrating GenAI into educational settings. The goal is to provide evidence-based recommendations for practice and identify key research directions and challenges for the future of CSCL in the context of GenAI.

Findings indicated that the tool could offer support in various aspects of design thinking.

papers.title: Appropriate Reliance in Human-AI Collaborative Problem-Solving: The Role of Critical Thinking
papers.authors: Chenyu Hou, Gaoxia Zhu, Vidya Sudarshan
papers.abstract: Reliance behaviors describe the frequencies and ways that people use AI tools for tasks such as problem-solving. There is a rising concern that students are over-reliant on Generative AI so that their critical thinking are being compromised. The notion of strategy- graded reliance argues that reliance behaviors are affected by a cognitive process in which an individual evaluates AI’s performance against human performance. We use critical thinking to capture this cognitive process. By analyzing 808 survey responses, including students’ critical thinking disposition, critical thinking skills, and reliance behaviors during a collaborative problem-solving task among undergraduate students, we find that collaborative, reflective, and cautious use of Generative AI is positively related to critical thinking. Therefore, we further conclude that desirable reliance on human-AI collaborative problem-solving is characterized by collaborative, reflective, and cautious use of Generative AI.

papers.title: Generative Failure: Learning Design in Programming with Generative
papers.authors: Hideki KONDO, Sayaka TOHYAMA, Shuntaro ISERI, Masaaki Ishii
papers.abstract: This study proposes the Generative Failure Method (GFM) to address challenges in applying Productive Failure to novice programming. Beginners often struggle with syntax errors, rarely compare diverse solutions, and lack tasks aligned with interests. Leveraging large language models (LLMs), GFM helps novices overcome initial barriers, adapt project goals, and incrementally cultivate open-ended exploration. Rather than imposing open-ended tasks, GFM expands problem contexts as learners progress. A pilot study found that LLM support enabled learners to produce functional applications, engage in iterative trial-and-error, and reframe “failure” as a constructive resource for learning.

papers.abstract: This DBR study (n=33) explored human-AI collaborative patterns and how teacher- GAI collaboration can be optimized for knowledge building in STEAM teaching designs. The results indicated (1) four categories of human-AI collaboration: Operator-Supplier, Apprentice- Mentor, Ally-Ally and Agent-Producer. (2) Constructive use of GAI with community-based principle facilitated teachers’ knowledge building on prompting strategies and intention, making collaboration between teachers a conducive design principle to prove more productive interaction between teachers and GAI in the teaching design. (3) Implications for human-AI interactions are discussed.
