papers.title: Designing an AI-Powered Reflective Partner: Translating Self-Regulated Learning Theory into Generative Chatbot Scaffolds
papers.authors: Na Liu, John Nietfeld
papers.abstract: This interactive tool paper presents the design and development of an AI-powered chatbot that scaffolds college students’ self-regulated learning (SRL). Grounded in Pintrich’s SRL framework and informed by meta-analytic evidence on effective SRL interventions, the chatbot is designed as a reflective learning partner that supports metacognitive monitoring, strategic deployment, and affective regulation. Using a design-based research (DBR) approach, this study explores how SRL theory can guide the development of generative AI–mediated interactions. We describe the theoretical rationale underlying the tool, articulate key design principles, present the prototype’s architecture, and discuss implications for improving evidence-based, equitable AI scaffolds to enhance undergraduate learning outcomes.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Designing an AI-Powered Reflective Partner: Translating Self-Regulated Learning Theory into Generative Chatbot Scaffolds. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Making Collaborative Creativity Visible: The Viacocrea Dashboard
papers.authors: Manoli Pifarré, Maria Sitjà, Ihtesham Hussian
papers.abstract: Addressing complex global challenges requires learners to engage in cocreative processes and regulate their contributions at both individual and group levels. However, supporting and visualizing such multifaceted collaboration is difficult. Building on our previous work and the Viacocrea platform, which guides students through cocreation, we have developed the Viacocrea Dashboard—an interactive tool that visualizes group cocreation dynamics and computes creativity indicators using Natural Language Processing and learning analytics. Key metrics are developed that include fluency (idea quantity), flexibility (topic diversity), elaboration (idea richness), and originality (novelty). The dashboard helps students reflect on and regulate their work, draw inspiration from peers, and enhance cocreation strategies, while providing teachers with actionable insights for feedback and support. In this demo, we will present the Viacocrea dashboard, invite the audience to engage in interactive demonstrations, and discuss how Viacocrea can advance the orchestration of collaborative creativity in education.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Making Collaborative Creativity Visible: The Viacocrea Dashboard Manoli Pifarré draw inspiration from peers. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Supporting Classroom Orchestration and Collaborative Programming with Jupyter Analytics
papers.authors: Zhenyu Cai, Richard Lee Davis, Roland Tormey, Pierre Dillenbourg
papers.abstract: Jupyter notebooks have been widely adopted in STEM courses that have programming or data science integrated. Jupyter Analytics, a learning analytics system, has been built to provide teachers with visibility into student activity. In combination with its existing functions as an awareness and reflection tool, this demo illustrates how the new code- sharing feature can address the real needs of both instructors and learners within Jupyter notebooks. Specifically, we discuss its potential value in two use cases: (1) supporting teachers in orchestrating live-coding lectures, and (2) helping students merge and synchronize work in collaborative programming. This covers two common pedagogical contexts in higher education: teacher-led lectures and student-centered active learning environments with group projects or collaborative sessions.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: S upporting Classroom Orchestration and Collaborative Programming with Jupyter Analytics. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Learning from the Experts: Exploring Human–AI Feedback through Expert-AI
papers.authors: Tomoki Takizawa, Masahiro Ogino, Maki Sakurai
papers.abstract: This demo introduces Expert-AI, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to emulate aspects of human experts’ reasoning and feedback. Drawing on experts’ writings, lectures, and interviews, the system provides dialogic, context-sensitive feedback grounded in expert perspectives, allowing experts to review and refine responses over time. We report preliminary findings from a pilot study in a business idea creation course at a private university in Japan, where students used both Expert-AI and general-purpose generative AI systems (e.g., ChatGPT). The findings suggest complementary roles: students used Expert-AI for conceptual framing and strategic evaluation, and general-purpose generative AI for elaboration and implementation planning. These findings suggest learners’ interpretations of AI feedback may vary depending on how it is presented. Accordingly, the demo presents the text version of Expert-AI alongside early multimodal prototypes including voice and android embodiments to examine how interaction modality shapes perceived credibility, empathy, trust, and engagement in expert-like AI feedback.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Learning from the Experts: Exploring Human–AI Feedback through Expert-AI. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: SciStory: A Demo of AI-Supported Socioscientific Learning through Visual Novels
papers.authors: Megan Humburg, Joshua Danish, Yeo Jin Kim, Morgan Vickery, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Namrata Srivastava, Sarah Burriss, Krista Glazewski, James Lester
papers.abstract: Our tool demo will explore intersections between narrative-centered learning, AI agents as inquiry scaffolds, and the interdisciplinary exploration of socioscientific issues. We will share our current design of SciStory: Pollinators, an interactive visual novel designed to support middle grades students in developing persuasive arguments to solve socioscientific problems in their community. Discussion will explore how we balance ethical issues around generative AI in our agent design, leverage co-design practices to iteratively improve collaborative game features, and draw on principles from problem-based learning to engage learners in developing solutions for complex socioscientific issues.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: SciStory: A Demo of AI-Supported Socioscientific Learning through Visual Novels. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: CLUE: A Learning-Goal Oriented AI-Enhanced STEM Inquiry System
papers.authors: Leslie Bondaryk, Ido Davidesco, Na’ama Y. Av-Shalom, Alden J. Edson
papers.abstract: Integrating AI into STEM classrooms risks shortcutting the productive struggle that makes inquiry-based learning effective. This session introduces CLUE, a collaborative platform that addresses this risk through rubric-centered AI personalization: rather than deploying generative AI as an open-ended chat interface, CLUE uses curriculum-tuned categorization rubrics to make student problem-solving strategies visible to both learners and teachers. In this way, CLUE’s rubric-centered approach operationalizes sensemaking for any particular curriculum. We conjecture that this design supports teacher noticing, promotes metacognitive reflection, and sustains productive struggle by shifting AI feedback away from answer-giving and toward strategy awareness and peer comparison. We will demonstrate several classroom- tested STEM curricula paired with these AI scaffolds, and attendees will participate in a live collaborative experience to see how CLUE's rubric-based approach makes AI-generated enrichment transparent and purposeful. The session will explore the design opportunities and challenges behind this methodology, invite discussion about alternative approaches, and share directions for future empirical evaluation. Attendees will leave with practical strategies for integrating AI into STEM classes and access to CLUE tools for use in their own classrooms.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: CLUE: A Learning-Goal Oriented AI-Enhanced STEM Inquiry System. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: CoDialogue Space: Design of AI-supported Collaborative Learning Platform
papers.authors: Eunhye Flavin, Kunal Mohindra, Jeonghyun (Jonna) Lee
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CoDialogue Space, a generative AI–supported collaborative learning platform that provides real-time facilitation during group dialogue. While computer- supported collaborative learning holds promise, it often depends on ad hoc analysis, scripted prompts, and static scaffolds. CoDialogue Space addresses these limitations through discursive facilitation strategies, multiuser–AI interaction, adaptive facilitation levels, and instructor- configurable prompts without requiring coding. We present its design features, offering a scalable, theoretically grounded environment for advancing AI-mediated collaborative learning.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: CoDialogue Space: Design of AI-supported Collaborative Learning Platform. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: TopoLA Dashboard: Making Topological Learning Analytics Accessible for Exploring Learner Behavioral Structure
papers.authors: Hitoshi Inoue, Koichi Yasutake
papers.abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) offers powerful methods for understanding structural patterns in learner populations, yet its application in learning analytics remains an emerging field with limited interpretive precedent. This interactive demo presents TopoLA Dashboard, a tool designed to make topological learning analytics accessible to educators and researchers without requiring topology expertise. By applying Zigzag Persistent Homology to behavioral data from the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, the dashboard tracks —the number of connected behavioral components—across the course timeline, alongside composite indicators TEWI and TSI. We connect these constructs explicitly to CSCL concepts i𝛽𝛽n 0 cluding social cohesion and co-regulated learning, while foregrounding a critical interpretive distinction: apparent convergence may reflect learner attrition rather than genuine behavioral alignment. Rather than providing definitive interpretations, the dashboard employs a three-layer framework—objectiv𝛽𝛽e 0 metrics, research-grounded pattern descriptions, and reflective prompts—to support educator sensemaking. We illustrate this framework with an authentic OULAD course example, demonstrating how rising and TEWI values in the weeks preceding an assessment deadline can prompt targeted instructional reflection. Participants will explore authentic OULAD data, experiment with topolo𝛽𝛽g 0 ical parameters, and discuss design implications for emerging structural analytics.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: TopoLA Dashboard: Making Topological Learning Analytics Accessible for Exploring Learner Behavioral Structure. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Show Your Work: A Gentle Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks for K-12 Educators
papers.authors: Michelle Hoda Wilkerson, Sun Young Ban, Jacob Shin, Xiaoyue Zhang
papers.abstract: We are developing a suite of free, web-based, asynchronous introductory Jupyter notebooks designed for K-12 educators with little to no prior experience with programming or with computational notebooks. In contrast to typical “intro notebooks” which focus on technical features, the Show Your Work project builds on theory and findings from the learning sciences and science education to introduce computational notebooks as epistemic tools within specific school subject domains, guiding educators to explore the questions: What role can notebooks play in my specific classroom? What does it feel like to conduct an investigation using a Jupyter notebook? What epistemic and communicative practices are foregrounded and backgrounded by computational notebooks? These materials are likely of interest to ISLS members who work in computing education, computing-integrated STEM education, and/or teacher education, as well as to members who wish to learn more about computational narrative as a new area of focus within the learning sciences. Motivation Jupyter notebooks are a form of computational notebook, an artifact that allows multiple blocks of editable, executable code and its output to be interspersed with rich text in a single document in the spirit of Knuth’s “literate programming” (Knuth, 1984). The name, “Jupyter,” evokes three computer languages commonly associated especially with data analysis – Julia, Python, and R (Perez & Granger, 2015). Since its original release about a decade ago, Jupyter notebooks now support a wide variety of computational languages (Granger & Perez, 2021). While it is not the first example of computational notebooks, Jupyter has been widely adopted due to its availability as a free and open source tool, and the Jupyter infrastructure now forms the foundation of a variety of popular interactive computing environments such as Google Colab and Deepnote. Although they were originally developed as a scientific research and communication tool, there is growing interest in using Jupyter notebooks at the K-12 level. Several research projects have studied the integration of Jupyter notebooks into secondary and intro college instructional materials (Fleischer et al., 2022; Son et al., 2021; Van Dusen, 2020). They are also becoming adopted as a curricular infrastructure including as part of Berkeley’s popular Data 8 “Introduction to Data Science” course activities (data6.org; data8.org), UCLA’s CourseKata high school mathematics curriculum (coursekata.org), and ProDaBi, a data/AI curricular package for secondary students (www.prodabi.de/en/). Most recently Jupyter Everywhere, a free, lightweight, simplified Jupyter interpreter interface that makes it easy for teachers and students to launch, edit, and share Jupyter notebooks without installing special software or services (jupytereverywhere.org). Jupyter notebooks, as a popular example of a broader genre of computational notebooks, are likely to be of particular interest to the Learning Sciences community for theoretical reasons. In a recent paper, Odden and Zwickl (2025) described Jupyter notebooks as an example of diSessa’s notion of computational literacy: highlighting their integration of the material dimension of computational literacy through its support for explicit executable code, the cognitive (epistemic) dimension through users’s ability to test, revise, and keep note of the discoveries they make as they examine the output of their code, and the social (communicative) dimension through the ability to share this blend of code with text, images, and other explanatory media with others. However, there is growing evidence that additional support is needed for Jupyter notebooks to be productively leveraged in K-12 classrooms. Most existing work describes a variety of technical and conceptual difficulties that teachers and students encounter when working with computational notebooks (e.g., Hanč et al., 2020; Johnson, 2020). While the potential for deep epistemic engagement through computational exploration and communication is high (Hüsing et al., 2024), without careful design or preparation notebooks are at risk of surface- level engagements in which students simply execute embedded code and read the output as if it were a printed text. T he need for teacher professional development Beyond the need to address the technical challenges for teachers that are already well-documented in the literature, it is also important to offer pedagogical and epistemological support when introducing new epistemic tools in curricular materials. Ample work has demonstrated that introducing even “authentic” tools in secondary classrooms is only valuable to the extent that they are understood by teachers and students to support sensemaking (Stroupe et al., 2019). For example, students who are asked to use agent-based models to explore the particulate nature of matter are only successful insofar as they identify some compatibility between their representation of the phenomenon and the affordances of the tool (Wilkerson et al., 2018). Inspired from Russ’ (2014) distinction between epistemology “of” science versus epistemology “for” science, here we might similarly articulate computing not only as a practice “of,” but also “for” scientific reasoning. Teachers play a critical role in helping students recognize the potential benefits of a given computational tool for advancing their understanding (Wagh et al., 2025). Thus to maintain disciplinary depth and support all students, teachers need to clearly understand the learning goals that a given activity or tool is meant to support, and be able to notice and respond to student thinking in service of those goals (Robertson et al., 2015). A first step to supporting such understandings is to examine how teachers, as learners themselves, might experience computational notebooks as a sensemaking tool. Even if teachers do recognize the ways in which computational notebooks might function as an epistemic tool, there are still possible ambiguities regarding exactly what aspects of the analysis of complex datasets they can support. This is because data investigations are naturally interdisciplinary, and therefore their role within the curriculum can be ambiguous (Finzer, 2013). There are a number of paths an investigation can take. For example, in our own prior work, we found that teachers might emphasize dramatically different aspects of a data visualization, for instance, focusing on scientific, social, or mathematical learning goals (Wilkerson et al., 2025); a practice consistent with broader findings suggesting that teachers significantly shape how materials are enacted in their classroom (Remillard & Heck, 2014). Thus demonstrating how Jupyter notebooks or other computational narrative tools might integrate into a variety of disciplines, with a variety of potential (e.g. computational, statistical, or content-oriented) goals is consistent with what we know about teachers’ data integration practices. Design principles To address the need for epistemologically and pedagogically oriented teacher professional development experiences, we are developing (with a cohort of approximately 30 pre-service and in-service teachers, using a judicious informant design approach; Scaife et al., 1997) a suite of computational notebooks intended to form the basis of an interactive, self-paced introduction to Python notebooks for K-12 classroom educators. Our rationale, building on the preliminary findings from research described above, is that many practicing teachers are being introduced to notebooks through their integration into curriculum, without time to familiarize themselves with not only the technical but also and more importantly with the epistemological and pedagogical dimensions of these tools. In a preliminary analysis of several existing “Introduction to Jupyter” notebooks developed both for practitioners and for educators, we identified an almost exclusive focus on their technical aspects. This included how a notebook can be run, edited, and what are some of its basic and advanced features. Several also included features that support pedagogical goals such as encouraging a tinkering disposition (“It is easy to break the code this way, but that is a normal part of coding!” from the YouCubed Jupyter introduction) or supporting the inquiry cycle (as demonstrated in CourseKata’s Jupyter introductory materials). Some existing introductory notebooks briefly addressed the epistemic role of notebooks in science, typically through appeals to authority. Building on these initial findings, our sequence of notebooks intentionally foreground the pedagogical potential of notebooks as an epistemic tool, as grounded within use cases across a variety of school subjects. Each notebook is designed to explicitly communicate about eight principles we identified as desirable in our review of existing introductory notebooks including the purpose of leveraging a computational notebook for an activity; providing a comparison to other tools that might be used in such an activity; modeling and encouraging documentation both of code and of users’ thinking; describing the planned use of specific or unique features of the notebook to aid in analysis; supporting specific code learning goals; supporting specific data learning goals; supporting specific content learning goals, and encouraging productive dispositions toward notebook use. Guided by these principles, our suite of notebooks provides teachers with repeated experiences in which they are expected to conduct inquiry using specific combinations of code, data, and content, and to encounter useful or unexpected findings in the process (see next section). As we make clear in our materials, our goal is not necessarily to advocate for the wholesale integration of notebooks into teachers’ work. Rather, as we state explicitly in our introductory notebook, we seek to “introduce [teachers] to what notebooks are, explore how they might be useful, and help [teachers] decide if they are right for [their] classroom.” (Intro Notebook). T he “Show York Work” suite of notebooks The “Show Your Work” sequence of activities is under active development, with five notebooks ready for sharing at the time of writing and an anticipated 10 ready by the time of the ISLS conference. When completed, the materials will include notebooks organized into four phases. Phase 1 provides a basic introduction and early data exploration experience using Jupyter notebooks. Phase 2 provides a variety of notebooks designed to introduce key code and data concepts that are most likely to be relevant to integrating Jupyter data explorations into particular school subjects such as chemistry, physics, statistics, and so on. For these first two phases, most materials are already well-developed and we are in the process of testing and refining them in collaboration with approximately 30 pre-service and in-service teachers. Phase 3 will include deeper dives into key computing and data concepts along with student case studies to encourage teacher noticing as mediated by Jupyter notebook interactions (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2017). Phase 4 will include materials to support teachers in adapting and creating their own notebooks for classroom use. This includes scaffolding their use of more traditional Jupyter documentation materials, and offering guidance on judicious use of generative AI tools, particularly those embedded in notebook development tools such as VSCode, whilst attending to the pedagogical and investigative principles introduced throughout the materials. These third and fourth phases are planned, though we anticipate that draft materials will be available for sharing by the time of the conference. Below, we elaborate on materials associated with Phase 1 and Phase 2 activities. Phase I: Introducing notebooks as computational narratives Our introductory notebook introduces teachers to the idea of a computational notebook as an “interactive lab notebook” in which they can keep, experiment with data and code, and communicate findings. The notebook guides teachers through the basic aspects of navigating, executing, and editing computational notebooks; diagnosing common errors and how to address them; and compares them to other epistemic tools used for data analysis in K-12 classrooms. Teachers then complete a data investigation activity using the well-known Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2020), in which they encounter an unexpected non-linear relationship between bill depth and bill length in a population of penguins, and use visualization to explore what other factors (e.g. sex, species, mass, age, etc.) may help explain the irregular distribution (Figure 1). Figure 1 Screenshots from The Introductory Notebook Including an introduction to notebooks (left), an inquiry activity (middle), and scatterplot code that users edit and supplement to address the inquiry question (right). Phase II: Targeting key code and data concepts through “Topic Bundles” The following set of notebooks focus on different disciplinary “bundles.” These are combinations of ideas from computing, data, and science that support specific kinds of subject matter explorations (such as GIS mapping to explore geological phenomena; exploring and visualizing basic descriptive statistics about distributions). Figure 2 features a notebook that introduces time series analysis through an exploration of air quality data as one such disciplinary “bundle.” The notebook introduces computational datetime as a specialised data structure, scaffolds users to generate and annotate lineplots, and to interpret time-series line plots with attention to scale, potential causes, and distinguishing between signal and noise. The notebook uses air quality data collected by local and national governmental organizations, and introduced related scientific concepts required to interpret patterns in the data (e.g. the Air Quality Index or AQI as a composite measure of air quality and PM2.5, Ozone, and Carbon Monoxide as specific air pollutants). through two interactive tasks. Figure 2 Screenshots of the Air Quality Notebook. The beginning segment introduces time series data and associated data structures and visualizations (left), and the major activity involves analyzing the different concentration patterns of three pollutants during a major fire event (right). We are developing similar notebooks that connect to core topics in statistics, physics, engineering, nad more (Table 1). For each, we work to identify one major phenomenon of interest for which patterns revealed through data and computing grant powerful insight into scientific mechanisms; 3-5 core code concepts that are required for the type of analysis that is introduced; and 3-5 data concepts related to the analysis. Table 1 Completed, in Progress (*), and Planned (^) Topic Bundles. Discipline Phenomenon Code Concepts Data Concepts Exploring patterns in air Time Series Data datetime Chemistry quality (AQI, Ozone, PM2.5, Scale lineplot CO) Distinguishing Signal from Noise Typicality across contexts of lists and dataframes Measures of center, spread, and Statistics test scores, housing prices histogram and boxplot typicality functions Linear regression Physics* Exploring force and motion scatterplot with fit line Residuals Optimizing the design of a data filters Optimization Engineering* cell phone Filtering English Sentiment analysis of focal strings Feature Extraction Language Arts^ texts frequency plots Bag of Words Interactive demo plan and accessing “Show Your Work” notebooks We look forward to possibly presenting this work at ISLS, which will allow us to learn from the community what might be other areas of need and to invite collaborators to contribute. By the time of the conference, we hope to have unified the notebooks into a single interactive digital interface that can be easily navigated, and we plan to have several laptops available for visitors to interact with the materials. Show Your Work project materials are being gradually released under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommerical 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) License, and some can be accessed at github.com/CalCoRE/show-your-work. papers.title: Designing a Dashboard for Insights into Complex Skills
papers.authors: Emily Kerzabi
papers.abstract: This paper describes the design and implementation of a functional prototype of a researcher-facing dashboard for insights into complex skills from multi-source data, including school records, chat/communication data, and item responses. Features include statistical insight panels and customizable layouts, incorporating visual cues (color coding by demographic variables) and flexible panel splitting for comparative analysis. Socio-Semantic Network Analysis (SSNA) maps student interactions and content mentions, revealing discourse patterns. The dashboard empowers researchers to uncover meaningful associations and generate analytic insights. Working with and visualizing multi-source, complex skill data Modern complex skill research generates rich datasets. Unlike dashboards designed for instructional decision- making or student self-monitoring, researcher-facing tools must support exploratory data analysis, hypothesis generation, and validation of constructs across diverse data types. The handling, cleaning, and linking of multi- source data can be an arduous undertaking, and tools to support researchers in easily viewing, manipulating, and testing their data are lacking. This paper describes a functional prototype to support researchers in their visualization and analysis of complex data. A study involving a collaborative social and emotional learning (SEL) curriculum (Hao et al., in press) provides the motivating context for developing and testing a flexible and user- friendly data dashboard, with the heart of a data explorer. The study collects various data, including conversation (chat) text from small groups of students, time on screen, and individual responses to teacher questions and personal skill reflections (using different item types and collected during SEL lessons). Simultaneously, researchers collect student school records, including pre/post academic outcomes, student self-report ratings on their social and emotional health, and teacher observations of student SEL skills. With these diverse types of collected data, it is both a challenge and an opportunity to think through and plan exploratory data analyses and data visualizations that may elicit insight into the targeted complex skill. Existing dashboards often focus on teacher, school, or student use; however, unlike teachers or students, researchers often work with multi-source datasets that require complex wrangling, integration, and statistical modeling, and should be guided by the educational learning theories that are the foundation of the research investigation (Wise & Shaffer, 2015). This project addresses the gap for an analyst-oriented analytics platform for investigating complex skills. The foundation for the proposed researcher-facing data dashboard is customizability of data visualizations, which can alert an attentive analyst to dig more deeply into the dataset(s) in meaningful ways. Based on data handling strategies proposed by Nicolini (2012), Goodyear (2020, p. 1052) advocates for “zooming in” and “zooming out” of data, to allow the broad patterns observable in high level data to trigger deeper analysis, and vice versa. The author argues that this capability is essential for generating actionable insights. Goodyear’s 2020 paper on co-configuration in hybrid learning spaces (such as this case of the SEL classroom), and suggests that analytic tools should support iterative refinements, adjustments, and even personalization of their data analysis environment. This approach is particularly relevant for dashboards designed to work with complex, multi- source datasets. To handle and link multi-source data, Bakharia et al. (2020) advocate for using star schema architecture (a powerful and versatile data structure commonly used in business analytics and data warehouses; see Microsoft Ignite, 2024) to organize and group data, allowing for aggregate calculations on grouped variables for various timeframes. Using this architecture, comparative analyses can target specific variables across the dataset that are expected to interact with other variables in meaningful ways based on relevant learning theories. The authors’ work highlights the need for dashboards that allow researchers to correlate diverse data types (e.g., process data, survey outcomes, academic measures) to surface statistically significant relationships, outliers, and group differences. Rather than conducting blind omnibus tests of significance across the various data components, this approach avoids the risk of false positives and misinterpretation that can arise from testing everything without context, and it aligns with the dashboard’s designed features, such as statistical insight panels and customizable visualizations. In addition to traditional statistical analyses and representations, student chat and communication data can be visualized using Socio-Semantic Network Analysis (SSNA). De Liddo et al. (2011) describes a discourse network structure consisting of a concept network (chat content) and a social network (human nodes), which are assumed to be strongly connected. The aim of De Liddo et al.’s discourse-centric learning analytics is to logically c onnect students to the content of learning, thereby providing meaningful insight into what students learn, at what point, and with whom. As further proof of concept, Zhu and Chen (2023) prototyped a similar SSNA model in their Joint Attention-Interaction-Creation framework and were able to effectively model how ideas are generated in collaborative discourse. By integrating an SSNA framework into the dashboard design, this project aims to move beyond static representations of simple correlations and statistical tests to offer researchers a dynamic, interactive environment for exploring complex relationships in SEL data. Finally, because the dashboard is inherently visual, best practices in visual data communication should be followed. Franconeri et al. (2021) offer many concrete insights on how to communicate with data effectively so that data insights become clear. The authors recommend thinking first about the goal of the displayed data; for example, use connected lines to show a continuum of connected data (e.g., avoid bars for time series) to encourage users to see trends over time. One goal of good data visualization is to reduce cognitive load for the data user, which ranges from including direct labels (or hover text) rather than relying on legends, to controlling comparisons with grouping or splitting options, such as the flexibility to view the data in side-by-side panels or overlays with color coding schema to distinguish groups. The authors strongly encourage respecting common conventions for spatial and visual channels (e.g., up for more and left to right for the passage of time), as well as avoiding using visual channels like length or area to plot purely categorical data. This also implies that nested data, such as students in classrooms or groups, follow hierarchical top-down structures to illustrate nested mappings. Following the best practices and analytic frameworks put forth by these studies has the potential to offer researchers a powerful, customizable environment for exploring and interpreting complex skill data. While the data to be used as a basis for this design is from a SEL hybrid-learning school environment, the design principles and practices are transferable to other complex sets of educational data to support actionable insights through dynamic visualization and data exploration tools.

papers.title: Declarative Narrative: Interactive Storytelling with Generative AI
papers.authors: Varun Bhatt, Chris Proctor
papers.abstract: Generative AI provides us with multiple challenges as well as opportunities. While it is disruptive to the field of writing instruction in some ways, it also allows us to innovate new genres of writing. We present three new interfaces for AI-supported writing, allowing an author of an interactive story to delegate detail, plot, and characterization to the AI while still maintaining narrative control of a story. This demo will present examples of interactive stories using these interfaces and allow participants to play through them, as well as write and share their own interactive stories.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Declarative Narrative: Interactive Storytelling with Generative AI Varun Bhatt. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Empowering Learner Agency in Writing with GenAI: A Web-based Platform
papers.authors: Ho Yin Fong, Chun Lai, Xiao Hu
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) have led to increasing attention in how chatbots and agentic tools may support students’ self-regulated learning (SRL). However, existing works primarily focus on short-term interventions on adult learners, offering limited insights into how GenAI can meaningfully foster SRL and learner agency in K-12 education. To address this gap, we introduce GAILA, a writing platform that integrates stage-specific AI agents with real-time learning analytics dashboards (LADs) to support the forethought, performance, and reflection phases of SRL. For students, GAILA offers structured writing workflows, task-aligned AI agents, and real-time analytics to encourage informed self- monitoring and behavioral adjustments. For teachers, GAILA provides fine-grained configurations of writing stages and agent visibility for pedagogical control. Together, these features enable sustained, classroom-integrated use of GenAI tools and open opportunities for research on how GenAI can support SRL among secondary school students.

papers.title: Designing the Next Generation of Computational Modeling and Learning with AI
papers.authors: Tamar Fuhrmann, Line Have Musaeus, Ole Sejer Iversen, Paulo Blikstein
papers.abstract: As generative AI rapidly transforms how humans interact with computation, it challenges the foundations of many educational technologies designed to teach coding, modeling, and computational thinking. Systems that were once built around writing or arranging code—whether block-based or text-based—now coexist with tools that generate programs through natural language. This workshop invites the learning sciences and design research community to collectively explore how educational technologies that include coding must be re-envisioned in light of these shifts. What will it mean to “code,” “debug,” or “model” when AI becomes a co-author? How might our existing environments—like MoDa, a block-based modeling platform, or text-based NetLogo simulations—need to be rethought for an era where learners reason through prompts, outputs, and model interpretation rather than syntax and structure? Our goal is to identify key design principles, challenges, and opportunities to guide the next generation of AI-powered computational learning environments. Theoretical background and significance Integrating computational thinking (CT) into science education equips students with powerful tools to explore scientific phenomena, foster deeper conceptual understanding, and engage in authentic scientific practices. The interdisciplinary potential of this work empowers students and practitioners to engage meaningfully with emerging local and global challenges (Barr et al., 2011; Weintrop et al., 2016). Existing literature identifies several core CT practices: abstraction, generalization, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debugging (Caeli & Yadav, 2020). Computational modeling, including agent-based modeling (ABM), has long been recognized as a valuable tool that can simultaneously support students' science learning and CT (e.g., Wilkerson et al., 2015; Musaeus et al., 2023; Musaeus et al., 2022). Recently, however, developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced new possibilities for how learners and educators may interact with computational models (Chen et al., 2023). In the future, it may no longer be necessary to write code to create scientific computer models, putting learners in the role of collaborators with generative AI. For decades, coding has served as both a tool for learning and a language for thinking (Papert, 1980; diSessa, 2000). Block-based and text-based environments embody constructionist ideals, empowering learners to express, test, and refine ideas through computation. Yet today, this paradigm is shifting. AI’s ability to generate executable code from natural language redefines what it means to “speak computation.” As we transition from programming languages to prompting, foundational concepts—such as loops, conditions, and agents—risk becoming invisible. At the same time, new epistemic practices emerge: prompt engineering, iterative interpretation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning about algorithmic agency. This timely workshop for the field of learning sciences demands that we rethink not only curricula, but also what fundamental concepts in programming that we still need to teach and how to design the tools themselves; how they mediate learning, distribute agency, and scaffold understanding when code is no longer the learner’s sole artifact of construction. Organizing team Line Have Musaeus leads research at the Center for Computational Thinking & Design, focusing on computing education, computational modeling, and STEM learning. Her work explores how integrating computational thinking into school subjects supports both student learning and teacher development. She co-designed CoTinker and has extensive experience organizing workshops on computing and AI in education. Tamar Fuhrmann leads research at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab at Teachers College, Columbia University. She is a founding leader of the MoDa project, focusing on computational modeling in science education. Her work integrates STEM, AI, and constructionist approaches, and she regularly leads professional development and international collaborations. Paulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Columbia University and director of the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. His research focuses on using technology to t ransform learning in STEM and AI. He founded the FabLearn program and has received major awards, including the NSF CAREER and AERA Early Career Award. Ole Sejer Iversen is a professor at Aarhus University and director of the Center for Computational Thinking & Design. His research focuses on computational empowerment, helping young people become active creators of technology. He works at the intersection of participatory design, computing education, and policy, leading large-scale international projects. Workshop goals and intended audience This workshop is designed for researchers, designers, and educators in the learning sciences, computing education, and educational technology who are exploring the future of computational learning in the age of AI. It will particularly interest those developing or studying coding-based environments—such as block-based, text-based, or modeling tools—and those investigating how generative AI transforms students’ epistemic, creative, and design practices. Participants with backgrounds in design-based research, computational modeling, or AI in education will find opportunities to share perspectives, contribute to collaborative redesign activities, and help shape a research agenda for rethinking the role of coding and modeling in AI-mediated learning environments. Outline of planned activities and facility requirements The four-hour workshop (plus one hour for lunch and coffee) will begin with an opening and framing session (20 minutes) introducing key tensions in AI-integrated coding environments. This will be followed by case study provocations (40 minutes), during which participants engage with two computational modeling environments: MoDa, a block-based agent-based modeling tool, and CoTinker, a collaborative modeling environment. Participants will explore and design models while considering how these tools might evolve as learners use AI to generate, modify, and explain models. In the collaborative design challenge (60 minutes), small groups will reimagine an educational technology that includes coding, redesigning it to integrate AI while preserving learners’ epistemic and creative engagement. This will lead into a group synthesis and discussion (40 minutes), during which participants share insights, identify emerging principles, and surface tensions, producing a poster as the group outcome. The workshop will conclude with a closing reflection (20 minutes), focusing on articulating open research questions and opportunities for future collaboration. Participation requirements Participation is open to researchers, designers, educators, and graduate students interested in computational modeling, coding education, or AI-supported learning environments. No specific technical expertise or prior experience with educational learning environments is required. We would like to support a dynamic, collaborative environment in which multiple perspectives on the redesign of coding-based educational technologies can emerge. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past Over the past several years, ISLS conferences have hosted numerous workshops and symposia exploring computational modeling, data science education, and AI-supported learning, for example, Kafai et al., 2025; Wagh et al., 2024; Fuhrmann et al., 2022; Fuhrmann et al., 2024; and McElhaney et al., 2020. These events advanced theoretical and design frameworks for integrating computational practices into science and engineering education. However, few have directly addressed the implications of generative AI for redesigning the educational technologies that include coding, particularly how block-based and text-based modeling environments must evolve when learners can construct programs through natural language. This workshop builds on that lineage but reframes the central question: not how to teach coding, but how coding itself—and the tools built around it—should be reimagined for an AI-mediated future. By convening researchers working at the intersection of computational modeling, design-based research, and AI in education, the session extends ongoing ISLS dialogues toward a new design agenda: understanding how AI reshapes the epistemic and pedagogical foundations of computational learning tools. Expected outcome and outputs The workshop will strengthen a community of practice focused on designing tools that preserve human sense- making and agency alongside AI assistance. It will generate open-ended questions that help rethink computational educational technologies in an AI-mediated context, and build a shared vocabulary around emerging hybrid practices where coding, prompting, and modeling intersect. Rather than defining what the future of coding should be, the session aims to open a dialogue on how our tools—and our field—must evolve to meet it. papers.title: Integrating the Learning Sciences into Technical Infrastructure for the Future of AI in Education
papers.authors: Jeremy Roschelle, John Whitmer, Rene Kizilcec, Xin Wei
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential in education, attention must extend beyond AI applications to the technical infrastructure on which those applications depend. Datasets, models, benchmarks, and governance mechanisms are already shaping the future of educational AI, yet these foundational resources are often developed without sufficient engagement with the learning sciences. This workshop explores how learning scientists can contribute to the design of such infrastructural public goods in ways that better reflect what is known about learning, while also addressing concerns related to safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. By bringing together researchers working at the intersection of AI and learning, the workshop seeks to identify promising lines of work, articulate key tensions, and stimulate future collaboration on learning-science-informed AI infrastructure. Overview The learning sciences offer strong conceptual foundations for the design of educational AI, drawing on longstanding research on scaffolding, feedback, self-regulation, and collaboration (Quintana et al., 2004; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Järvelä et al., 2016; Sawyer, 2022). Yet these principles still only lightly shape the datasets, benchmarks, and model documentation on which AI systems depend. Training data rarely reflect what is known about productive learning interactions; benchmarks tend to measure task completion or factual accuracy rather than the quality of scaffolding or the depth of learner understanding; and model documentation seldom describes how a system's design relates to evidence on how people learn. Recent work by major AI developers signals growing interest in grounding educational AI in learning sciences principles (Jurenka et al., 2024; LearnLM Team, Google, 2025), but without more intentional integration into underlying infrastructure, educational AI risks prioritizing efficiency or engagement over meaningful support for learning. As past waves of "personalized learning" have shown, technology that optimizes for engagement without attending to how learning works can reproduce rather than address longstanding inequities in educational opportunity. This challenge is particularly pressing as new efforts seek to build openly shared educational AI resources as public goods. The K–12 AI Infrastructure Initiative, a five-year, $26 million effort led by Digital Promise and a coalition of partners, is funding the development of tutoring interaction corpora, learning-aligned benchmarks, and model documentation frameworks that embed pedagogical principles by design (Digital Promise, 2025; Roschelle et al., 2025). For such resources to genuinely advance learning, learning scientists must be actively involved in their co-design alongside AI engineers, education practitioners, and policymakers — contributing not only domain knowledge but also the critical perspectives needed to navigate questions of safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. This workshop therefore explores how the learning sciences can be systematically integrated into these infrastructural public goods. It brings together learning scientists, AI developers, education practitioners, and funders to examine where and how learning sciences expertise is most needed in the development of technical infrastructure for educational AI. Its goals are to inform participants about emerging infrastructure efforts and the role learning sciences can play in shaping them, create space for participants to share current work and articulate concerns, identify promising directions for future research and investment, and stimulate the formation of cross- sector collaborations. Building on recent ISLS programming on AI and education (International Society of the Learning Sciences, 2022, 2024), the workshop positions the learning sciences not only as a field that evaluates AI applications after they are built, but as one that can help shape the foundations on which educational AI is constructed. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108776462 GoGoData Participatory Sensing: Students, Educators and Researchers Building Collaborative Data Networks Charles Pimentel charlespimentel@ufrj.br Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) Vithoria Cabreira vithoriacabreira@gmail.com Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR) Walter Akio Goya, Paulo Blikstein, Renato Russo aag2197@tc.columbia.edu, paulob@tc.columbia.edu, renrusso@gmail.com Teachers College, Columbia University Arnan Sipitakiat arnan.s@cmu.ac.th Chiang Mai University Abstract: In this half-day workshop, participants will engage with GoGoData, an open learning plugin that connects the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) communication, and the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) to support participatory sensing and collaborative exploration of real-time data. Beyond experimenting with the plugin’s features for data collection, transmission, and interpretation, participants will analyze GoGoData as a design case that integrates constructionist principles with learning sciences perspectives on data literacy. Participants will, in turn, extend these theoretical and design lenses to examine how collaborative data networks can foster critical engagement with data in their own educational and research contexts. Proposers/Organizers Charles Pimentel Charles Pimentel is a Research Fellow at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, supporting the documentation of the GoGo Board and the development of data-focused learning activities. He holds a Master’s degree in Informatics from UFRJ and works in K-12 education with Programming, Artificial Intelligence, and Educational Robotics. Charles is a doctoral student at the Institute of Computing at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, researching Data Literacy, and a member of the FabLearn Fellows Cohort 3. He also teaches Design & Tech at Graded in São Paulo, developing tech-for-good projects connected to sustainability. Vithoria Cabreira Vithoria Cabreira is an undergraduate student in Computer Engineering at the Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR). She supports the development of digital tools and web technologies for educational and research projects. Her interests include software development, web platforms, and the creation of digital solutions that improve user experience. Vithoria is currently strengthening her technical skills through practical projects and experimentation with new technologies. Akio Goya Akio is an Educational Technology Designer for the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, coordinating the design, implementation, and documentation of GoGo Boards in Brazil, as well as the implementation of makerspaces in public schools. Akio holds a Master’s degree in Instructional Technology and Media from Teachers College, Columbia University (USA) and a Master’s and a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering from University of Sao Paulo (Brazil), and a Teacher Licensure in Mathematics (Middle and High School) from FIAR (Brazil). Paulo Blikstein P aulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Teachers College and an Affiliate Associate Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, where he directs the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab and the Lemann Center for Brazilian Studies. His research focuses on how new technologies can transform the learning of science, engineering and computation. Paulo is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading its research and development since 2001. Paulo has a Ph.D. from Northwestern University, a MSc. from the MIT Media Lab and an M.Eng. and B.Eng. from the University of São Paulo, Brazil. Renato Russo Renato is a doctoral candidate at the Technology, Media, and Learning program at Teachers College, Columbia University and a researcher at Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. In his research, Renato explores how learning technologies can promote critical and emancipatory knowledge construction practices. Renato earned a MA degree in Learning, Design and Technology from Stanford University Graduate School of Education. Arnan (Roger) Sipitakiat Arnan (Roger) directs the Teaching and Learning Innovation Center (TLIC) at Chiang Mai University in Thailand. As a faculty and researcher at the Computer Engineering Department, he also directs the Learning Inventions Laboratory (LIL). Arnan is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading research and development on the toolkit since 2001. Arnan focuses on designing technologically-rich learning tools, such as the GoGo Board, that have allowed students to explore areas including robotics, interactive art, games, agriculture, and community development. Arnan earned his MSc. and Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and B.Eng. from Chiang Mai University. Intended audience This workshop is intended for graduate students, educators, and researchers interested in exploring participatory sensing, critical data literacy, and learning technology design through hands-on experimentation. It particularly welcomes those studying or developing tools that connect physical computing, IoT, and real-time data exploration to promote collaborative inquiry and learning. More broadly, the session is open to all participants interested in integrating constructionist and learning sciences perspectives into the design of educational technologies. (Note that GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP are open-source platforms.) Duration of the event Half-day (3-4 hours, flexible depending on conference scheduling demands). Description of the event The GoGo Board was invented in 2001 as a low-cost and learner-friendly robotics and scientific sensing platform. In the years since, the project has undergone several design iterations, each affording new possibilities for students across diverse ages and backgrounds to explore powerful ideas in computing and STEM. In this workshop, participants will also engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that connects the GoGo Board to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data communication and visualization. CODAP, developed by the Concord Consortium, has a long-standing history as an open-source environment for data analysis and modeling that supports inquiry-based learning. Together, GoGoData, the GoGo Board Kit version 7, and CODAP create a participatory sensing ecosystem that enables students to collect, share, and interpret live data while examining the learning sciences principles underlying the design of these tools [1-3]. Workshop Format The workshop will be organized into five main activities. I - Historical framing. Participants will begin with a brief discussion on the evolution of tangible interfaces within the Learning Sciences and basic education contexts. This discussion will be situated alongside the rise of big data practices and participatory or crowd sensing, showing how learner-generated, real-time data from distributed sensors can reshape inquiry, evidence making, and classroom discourse. The framing will surface design lessons on openness, transparency, and agency, linking data practices to issues of provenance, privacy, and ethics, and highlighting how collaborative data networks can support critical engagement and community action. II - Exploring the GoGo Board 7 / GoGoData / CODAP. Participants will explore the core features of the GoGo Board version 7 and the GoGoData plugin, examining how each component emerged from research data and i terative design decisions. Using onboard controls, they will visualize sensor values, directly before connecting to a computer to interact with GoGoData and its integration with the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP). Through this connection, participants will experience how real-time sensor data can be collected, transmitted, analyzed, and explored within CODAP’s interactive environment. Facilitators will highlight how each feature embodies specific design principles that link tangible experimentation with data-driven inquiry. III - Participatory sensing exploration. Participants will collaboratively select a variable to measure, such as temperature, luminosity, pollution, or sound level, using a GoGo Board 7 kit sensor. Working in small groups, they will connect the GoGo Board to CODAP through the GoGoData plugin and deploy sensors in different internet-connected areas across the UCI campus. Each group will collect and share real-time data through the open-source plugin integrated with the data analysis platform, contributing to a collaborative network of distributed measurements. As data accumulate, participants will analyze emerging patterns across locations, drawing inferences about environmental or contextual factors. The activity will conclude with a collective discussion where groups interpret their findings, reflect on methodological decisions, and connect their insights to broader perspectives on participatory sensing, open data collaboration, and critical data literacy in education. IV - Conclusion and gallery walk. Participants will share and discuss the outcomes of their activities, reflecting on the lessons learned and insights gained throughout the workshop. The session will conclude with a collective show-and-tell, allowing groups to present their findings, highlight key observations from the participatory sensing exercise, and connect these experiences to broader questions about learning, design, and data literacy. V - Post-workshop interaction. Optional follow-up opportunities will be provided for participants who wish to continue collaborating after the session. These interactions may include online discussions, exchange of design ideas, and updates on future developments of the GoGoData platform. Participants will be invited to share reflections, resources, and potential research connections that extend the learning and collaboration initiated during the workshop. Throughout the workshop, facilitators will guide discussions connecting the design of GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP to learning sciences and constructionist frameworks, emphasizing how participatory sensing and data exploration are enhanced by open-source ecosystems. The session will highlight how openness, transparency, and accessibility in these tools empower learners and researchers to collaboratively collect, analyze, and interpret real-time data. Rather than serving as a technical training, the workshop offers a hands-on exploration of how open, theory-informed technologies developed through over twenty years of design-based research can foster agency, collaboration, and critical engagement with data. Participation requirements No requirements. We invite to join all participants interested in tangible interface design, educational robotics, and data science, irrespective of skill or experience levels. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past The author team conducted an NSF-funded project at the New York Hall of Science in collaboration with Teachers College, Columbia University, using the GoGo Board in data science camps for middle school students under the AISL program. We also did a physical computing workshop at ISLS 2024. Facilities and equipment required Facilities: ● Projector / screen for workshop facilitators ● Wifi connectivity Equipment: ● Gogo Boards Kits (board and sensors - we will provide them) ● Participants will be asked to bring their laptops with an available USB-C port. Minimal and maximal number of participants expected 8 - 15 participants Draft call for participation C alling all researchers, designers, and educators interested in exploring the power of participatory sensing to connect learning, data, and design. In this half-day workshop, you will engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that links the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data exploration. Together, these tools create a participatory sensing ecosystem where learners and researchers can collaboratively collect, share, and interpret live data (Figer 1). Beyond experimenting with the platform’s features, you will analyze GoGoData as a design case informed by constructionist and learning sciences perspectives, building on over two decades of iterative design research with the GoGo Board. This workshop offers a unique opportunity to experience how open-source technologies can empower communities to transform local data into meaningful insights and to apply these theoretical and design perspectives to your own educational research and development projects. Workshop format The workshop is planned for in-person delivery, with the option of hybrid participation if necessary. The program will include interactive, hands-on activities supported by remote contributions from members of the international workshop team, ensuring collaboration and engagement across locations. papers.title: An Evaluation Framework for Pedagogical Large Language Models
papers.authors: Eugene Park, Daniel Wendel, Grace Lin, Sharifa Alghowinem
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted as AI tutors, providing scalable, interactive assistance across a range of topics. Yet there remains a lack of a unified, comprehensive framework for evaluating the pedagogical behaviors these models exhibit across multiple tutoring sessions and varying learning scenarios. This workshop addresses this gap by introducing a two-layer evaluation framework that distinguishes between (1) foundational behaviors that LLMs must demonstrate to be considered pedagogically qualified, and (2) stylistic instructional behaviors that shape their effectiveness as tutors. Participants will refine and apply this framework through hands-on interactions with an LLM-powered tutoring system, engaging in a five-session sequence of introductory Python programming modules. Through this workshop, we aim to advance the application of generative AI tools in education settings in a safe and pedagogically effective manner. Organizers’ backgrounds Eugene Park is a software engineer and researcher in the Personal Robots Group at the MIT Media Lab, where he leads research and system development on LLM-powered AI tutoring platforms. His work focuses on large language models and AI safety with applications in education, and his research agenda is centered on building pedagogically effective and reliable AI tutors. Daniel Wendel is a lead software developer and research engineer in MIT’s Scheller Teacher Education Program. Daniel has served as a core developer, curriculum designer, and research manager on projects spanning agent-based modeling, virtual reality, and AI-mediated learning, and his work focuses on designing scalable learning technologies that strengthen STEM understanding through interactive computer-based environments. Dr. Grace C. Lin is a Learning Scientist and Assessment Designer at MIT whose work focuses on building children’s and students’ capacity to learn. As an educational researcher, Grace has led teams on educational intervention projects using innovative technology from cognitive training games to AI-powered conversational agents, and has contributed to building a practitioner-facing measures repository, particularly its rating systems, of early childhood measurements. More recently, her work has been focusing on child-centered AI, AI education for children and adults, the implications of AI technology, and its influences on human relationships. Dr. Sharifa Alghowinem is a leading research scientist in the field of multimodal AI and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). Currently stationed at MIT's Personal Robots Group, Dr. Alghowinem specializes in developing AI models to enhance human-robot interaction, with a particular focus on mood and behavior recognition using speech, gaze, and body movements to detect conditions such as engagement, depression and deception. Workshop theoretical background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as AI tutors, offering personalized explanations, adaptive feedback, and conversational guidance across a wide range of learning contexts. Their capacity to generate interactive, context-aware instruction positions them as promising tools for expanding access to high- quality tutoring, particularly in domains such as programming, where LLMs have demonstrated considerable competence. However, despite their growing use in classrooms and learning platforms, the learning sciences community lacks a principled understanding of how these models teach and which pedagogical behaviors support or hinder learning. Prior evaluations of AI tutors have typically focused on behavioral metrics that do not clearly distinguish between pedagogically harmful behaviors and those that are pedagogically effective (LearnLM Team et al., 2025; Macina et al., 2025; Maurya et al., 2025). While valuable, these metrics overlook a central insight from contemporary pedagogical theory: not all instructional traits are equally suitable across learning situations, nor do all teaching styles promote learning in the same way. Friesen & Su (2023) argue that pedagogy is not a fixed set of methods or universally “correct” practices, but rather a context-dependent negotiation between competing pedagogical tensions, such as constraint versus freedom, proximity versus distance, and protection versus exposure. Pedagogy, in this view, “is structured not so much by processes, methods, and outcomes, but by i rresolvable oppositions and the tensions between them”. This perspective highlights that effective teaching cannot be reduced to a single optimal style; instead, instructional behaviors must flexibly align with learners’ needs, contexts, and developmental stages. Bringing this lens to AI tutors underscores the need for an evaluation framework that differentiates essential pedagogical requirements from stylistic instructional variations, ensuring models are assessed not only for pedagogically correct behavior but also for their alignment with pedagogically effective behavior. Moreover, due to increasing domain expertise of frontier LLMs, this can create an illusion of overestimation in their pedagogical performance (e.g. strong performance on programming tasks or reasoning benchmarks may not necessarily translate to an LLM’s ability to teach effectively). A lack of a concrete analysis of LLMs’ pedagogical behaviors risks the misuse of LLMs, and prevents researchers and practitioners from meaningfully developing the instructional quality and reliability of AI tutors. To address this gap, we identified pedagogically harmful behaviors in LLM tutors, such as conceptual inconsistencies, topic drift, and failures to detect misconceptions, and formalize these issues as forms of pedagogical misalignment. Ensuring the absence of such behaviors represents a minimal requirement for safe and trustworthy AI tutoring. Building on this foundation, we introduce a two-layer evaluation framework for pedagogical alignment. The first layer, pedagogical qualification, captures whether an LLM satisfies baseline standards of instructional safety. The second layer, pedagogical personality, characterizes stylistic instructional traits, such as scaffolding depth, adaptivity, metacognitive prompting, and instructional tone, that shape the learning experience and likely modulate learning gains. This workshop aims to refine and operationalize this framework, deepen our shared understanding of pedagogical traits in AI tutors, and collaboratively develop metrics for evaluating them. Through hands-on interaction with an LLM-powered tutoring system, participants will explore how pedagogical safety and pedagogical style intersect, and how these dimensions can inform the design of reliable, aligned, and learning- effective AI-based educational tools. Intended audience and logistics This workshop is designed for researchers and practitioners in educational technology, the learning sciences, AI/ML, and NLP who are interested in the reliable and effective use of generative AI for education. It is particularly relevant for scholars studying AI safety, AI in education, human-AI interaction, or instructional design, as well as developers building LLM-powered educational tools. The workshop is planned as a full-day event to allow sufficient time for hands-on interaction with the LLM-based tutoring system across multiple sessions, group analysis and annotations of pedagogical behaviors, and structured discussions aimed at refining the proposed evaluation framework. To support effective collaboration, we request a room equipped with round tables suitable for small- group work. If possible, we also request basic writing materials, such as sticky notes, paper, pens, and colored markers. Participants will be asked to bring their own laptops to interact with the AI tutor. The workshop is designed for a minimum of 8 and a maximum of 30 participants, ensuring meaningful interaction, hands-on guidance, and productive group collaboration. Outline of planned activities The workshop is organized as a full-day, highly interactive session combining hands-on experience with an AI tutoring system, individual analysis, and structured group discussions. Participants will engage in five short introductory Python programming sessions using an LLM-powered tutor, evaluate the tutor’s pedagogical behaviors, and collaboratively refine the proposed two-layer evaluation framework. Schedule 09:00 – 09:30: Welcome and Introductions. (30 minutes) 09:30 – 10:40: Hands-on Interaction with AI Tutor: Modules 1–3. (70 minutes) 10:40 – 11:00: Break (20 minutes) 11:00 – 13:00: Hands-on Interaction with AI Tutor: Modules 4–5. Behavior Survey. (100 minutes) 13:00 – 14:00: Lunch Break (60 minutes) 14:00 – 15:30: Small-Group Annotation and Framework Refinement (90 minutes). 15:30 – 15:45: Break (15 minutes). Transition to whole-group synthesis. 15:45 – 17:00: Large-Group Discussion and Synthesis (75 minutes). 1 7:00 – 17:30: Closing Reflections and Next Steps (30 minutes). Expected outcomes and contributions This workshop will equip participants with a refined and practically grounded framework for evaluating the pedagogical behaviors of LLM-powered tutors. Through hands-on interaction with an AI tutoring system, individual and collaborative annotation exercises, and structured group discussions, participants will collaboratively sharpen the distinction between pedagogical qualification, the foundational behaviors required for safe and trustworthy tutoring, and pedagogical personality, the stylistic instructional traits that influence learning effectiveness. The workshop will produce a consolidated set of pedagogical metrics, including clarified definitions, improved categorizations, and a consensus-based ranking of behaviors along a harmful–to–stylistic spectrum. This refined framework and metric set will support future empirical research and systematic tool development practices. Beyond methodological contributions, the workshop will foster a shared vocabulary and conceptual grounding for analyzing how LLM tutors behave across different learning scenarios. Participants will gain insight into the strengths and limitations of current AI tutoring systems, enabling them to better identify problematic behaviors, understand instructional variability, and connect model behaviors to established learning sciences theory. Thus, this workshop also aims to strengthen the research community at the intersection of AI education and AI safety by identifying open challenges and catalyzing collaborations across the learning sciences, AI/ML, and educational technology domains.
