papers.title: A CSCL Taxonomy Building Workshop
papers.authors: Martin Greisel, Burcu Şener, Sebastian Simon, Conrad Borchers, Elham Tajik, Bahar Shahrokhian
papers.abstract: This workshop aims at collaboratively developing a shared taxonomy for the Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community that captures diverse epistemological, methodological and technological perspectives to help build a common ground for CSCL research. Through pre-workshop Delphi input, hands-on application, and iterative refinement, participants co-construct a framework to support clearer communication, cumulative knowledge building, and more transparent dissemination in CSCL proceedings and journals. The resulting taxonomy and follow-up activities aim to strengthen community identity, foster collaboration, and guide future CSCL research and publication practices. Organizers ● Martin Greisel: Assistant professor/postdoc at the University of Augsburg, focusing on regulation in collaborative learning, peer feedback, and teacher training. ● Burcu Şener: Lecturer at Middle East Technical University, PhD candidate at Bogazici University, focusing on collaborative problem solving, collaborative debugging, computational thinking. ● Sebastian Simon: Postdoctoral fellow at the University of Le Mans with a PhD in Computer Science. During his PhD, he focused on enhancing mobile and co-located Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning with Augmented Reality (AR). In his current Postdoc position, he investigates generative AI agents as collaborative entities in co-located CSCL settings. ● Conrad Borchers: PhD candidate at Carnegie Mellon University, researching data science and HCI applications to improve educational processes. ● Elham Tajik: PhD student at the University at Albany, she focuses on the transformative role of generative AI in education and HCI. ● Bahar Shahrokhian: PhD candidate at Arizona State University, researching multimodal learning analytics and collaboration in co-located learning environments. Intended audience and resources This half-day workshop is intended for all researchers and educators interested and engaged in CSCL, as well as its related domains, including but not limited to: educational psychologists, computer scientists and learning scientists. We particularly welcome researchers from all domains to contribute their vision of computer-supported collaborative learning, with a minimum of 8 to a maximum of 40 participants. We can manage up to 30 in-person and 10 online (Zoom) participants. Regarding resources, we only need a large seminar room with WiFi and a projector that enables group work through flexible tables (i.e., no lecture hall with fixed rows). In-person participants will be asked to bring their personal laptops. Description of the event Theme and goals In recent years, the field of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) has continued to expand in scope, methods, and theoretical foundations. While this diversity reflects the richness and vitality of the field, it also creates challenges for integration and cumulative knowledge building. Researchers draw on a wide range of epistemological, methodological, and technological perspectives, and often work in parallel rather than in concert. This fragmentation can make it difficult to identify shared concerns, trace the development of ideas, or recognize complementarities among approaches. At the same time, the multiplicity of perspectives represents an invaluable resource. If systematically understood and connected, this multiplicity can foster deeper insights into learning processes and the design of collaborative technologies. Previous CSCL workshops have identified the need for a common language across the different domains that are present in the CSCL community. Common language p resents the first step to common ground, a concept that is key to the knowledge building in a scientific community, particularly in one that emphasizes the strength of co-existing paradigms, requiring awareness of semiotic and semantic differences (that may otherwise lead to issues like gatekeeping or siloed research, Kuhn, 1962). Particularly, the 2025 CSCL workshop participants have identified the need for community building in the CSCL field and the potential of a collaboratively created CSCL taxonomy as an artefact for building common ground. Consequently, this workshop has two goals: (1) community building and (2) taxonomy development. To build community, the workshop brings together members of the CSCL community to overcome fragmentation and to harness the richness of the field’s diversity. It will help strengthen a community identity by creating an awareness of what constitutes CSCL and foster a feeling of agency through a common activity centered around the community itself (Wise & Schwarz, 2017). The second goal is to develop a taxonomy for classifying future CSCL research, especially contributions to future conference proceedings and ijCSCL articles. This taxonomy aims to offer a shared framework that reflects the community’s pluralistic character while enabling more coherent navigation, communication, comparison, and synthesis of research. As a tangible outcome and lasting artefact, it aims to promote collaboration across paradigmatic differences in the future. In addition, the process of developing such a taxonomy itself constitutes an effort of community building, thereby also serving the first goal of the workshop. In summary, by collaboratively developing and validating such a taxonomy, supported by a broad proportion of the CSCL community, the workshop seeks to lay the foundation for a more connected and integrated future for CSCL research. Theoretical background and relevance to the field and conference CSCL is inherently multidisciplinary, integrating perspectives from at least the learning sciences, educational sciences, psychology, and computer science. This diversity enriches the field but also introduces substantial variation in researchers’ underlying epistemic stances. According to the AIR model (Chinn et al., 2014), such stances encompass differences in 3 ways. First, researchers have different aims—they seek to achieve different things with their work. Second, they hold different ideals—they disagree on what counts as valid knowledge and good evidence and the criteria by which success is evaluated. Third, they use different reliable processes—they favor different methods for how data is created and interpreted, that is, the methods considered most appropriate to reach their aims. While this pluralism fosters innovation and theoretical breadth, it also poses challenges for mutual understanding in our field. Researchers examining similar phenomena may struggle to find, understand, and interpret each other’s research contributions because they pursue different aims, evaluate knowledge by different criteria, and employ different methods. This is reflected, for example, in the co-existence of different major theoretical traditions (e.g., constructivist and sociocultural, cognitive/information‑processing), a focus on different mid-level theories or theory-driven pedagogical frameworks (e.g., knowledge building, cognitive load theory, theory of immersive collaborative learning) or interactional constructs (e.g., transactivity, socio‑cognitive conflict) and competence frameworks (e.g., collaborative problem‑solving skills), and different analytical and design methodologies (e.g., collaborative analytics or design-based research) (Brown, 1992; Dillenbourg, 1999; Graesser et al., 2018; Kirschner et al., 2018; Makransky & Petersen, 2023; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014; Vogel et al., 2023; Vygotsky, 1978; Wise et al., 2023). As a result, communication across perspectives can become fragmented, leading to disciplinary silos and limited knowledge integration within the CSCL community (Wise & Schwarz, 2017), thereby hindering the advancement of knowledge. To remedy fragmentation, a workshop at the CSCL 2025 conference aimed at developing a shared paradigm (see also section “Relationship to similar events conducted in the past” below). However, one main outcome, also advocated by a panel of senior CSCL scholars, was that attempting to unify the CSCL community under a single theoretical or methodological framework would weaken the field’s richness in diversity. Its multi- perspectivity is not a weakness to be corrected, but a strength that enables deeper and more comprehensive inquiry. As a result, the goal should be to bridge epistemic diversity to enable constructive dialogue rather than to simply erase different perspectives and epistemologies. A step toward bridging these differences is to establish a shared vocabulary that enables researchers to articulate their approaches in a comparable manner (Wise & Schwarz, 2017). When organized systematically, such a vocabulary can take the form of a taxonomy—a structured set of dimensions and descriptors that capture from which viewpoint researchers approach their investigation, which phenomenon they study, and how they study it. A CSCL taxonomy could thus provide a common reference point for describing research aims,

papers.title: Re-envisioning Assessment Challenges and Opportunities in the Generative AI Era through CSCL
papers.authors: Carol Chan, Xiao Hu, Baruch Schwarz, Stephen M. Fiore, Wenli Chen, Jun Oshima, Manoli Pifarré
papers.abstract: Assessment in higher education faces unprecedented challenges, as generative AI now enables students to produce polished assignments in seconds. Many institutions have responded by reverting to pen‑and‑paper exams, a solution that mitigates some concerns but introduces other problems narrowing educational aims. This workshop provides a platform for collaborative exploration and dialogue of how CSCL can offer fresh perspectives and pathways for addressing these challenges and creating opportunities. Grounded in CSCL theory, design, and analytics, this workshop examines conceptualizing AI as a dialogic, collaborative partner; designing innovative assessments; assessing processes rather than products; and using collaborative analytics to support learning in AI‑enriched environments. Key issues for inquiry include: purpose of assessment, design and fine‑tuning of AI‑supported assessment, AI- powered multi-modal analytics and feedback, equity and diversity, researcher–teacher collaboration, ethics-privacy, and public discourse. Together, we work towards re‑envisioning assessment, synergizing research and practice, building collective knowledge and strengthening CSCL's impact and significance in the Gen AI era. Organizing team We are a group of CSCL researchers with shared interests in examining how CSCL can offer perspectives and directions for addressing assessment issues in higher education arising from the use of generative AI. Carol Chan conducts research on knowledge building, focusing on socio-cognitive-epistemic dynamics, reflective assessment, analytics, and teacher professional development. Xiao Hu’s research is on learning analytics, automated assessment and feedback, and AI in education. Her research includes collaborative writing facilitated by real-time analytics dashboards, multimodal learning analytics in collaborative maker activity, and analytics- supported writing in AI environments. Baruch Schwarz's research in CSCL focuses on argumentation, dialogue, and reasoning, particularly examining the roles of technology in boosting collaborative argumentation. Stephen Fiore conducts research on Human-AI teaming, focusing on collaborative cognition, including knowledge building when collaborating with AI, and the role of artificial social intelligence in assessing collaborative learning. Jun Oshima examines how knowledge-building discourse among undergraduate /graduate students can be supported by Generative AI, and examines their interactions with AI from a network-science perspective. Wenli Chen conducts research on human-AI collaboration to augment human learning by fine- tuning generative AI informed by learning sciences theories, developing AI-powered multi-modal learning analytics to assess students’ collaborative learning in classrooms. Manoli Pifarré' examines and designs dialogic, technology-enhanced pedagogies that foster co-creation processes focusing on how interactive technologies—empowered by artificial intelligence and multimodal learning analytics—can assess, visualize, and support group-based creative problem-solving. Intended audience ● CSCL researchers/ graduate students interested in collaboration, assessment and generative AI ● Researchers/graduate students from learning sciences working on generative AI related to assessment ● Higher-education instructors/practitioners navigating new assessment challenges in the AI era with interest in research-informed strategies and collaborative approaches. Duration A half-day workshop will be conducted as a HYBRID event, with onsite and remote participants connected by Zoom and online sharing tools. Participants may register to attend as onsite or virtual attendees. W orkshop description and goals We are facing a global assessment crisis in higher education with the widespread use of AI tools: students can generate polished assignments in seconds, fueling surface learning, plagiarism, and metacognitive laziness, and leading to reliance on ChatGPT (Fan et al., 2025). Public discourse highlights the seriousness of this shift—for example, Bloomberg (May 27, 2025) asked, “Does college still have a purpose in the age of ChatGPT?” Many universities have reverted to in‑person, pen‑and‑paper exams, which mitigate some risks but create others, curtailing the valuable educational goals of inquiry, problem-solving, and collaboration. This workshop is premised on the idea that CSCL is well-positioned to offer directions for rethinking assessment in higher education in the AI age (Schwarz et al., in press). We build on decades of CSCL research on assessing collaboration (Cress et al., 2021), extending to CSCL theory, design, and analytics for assessment practice. Traditional assessments emphasize final products (e.g., essays) that AI can replicate easily. Conversely, CSCL foregrounds collaborative processes (e.g., co‑construction, shared regulation) and CSCL designs such as argumentation, dialogic interaction and knowledge building, can offer new ways to scaffold and assess AI‑human collaboration. Beyond polished output, CSCL analytics can make learning‑collaboration processes visible for feedback and actionable improvement (Wise et al., 2021). This workshop provides a venue for sharing CSCL research and practices to address challenges and opportunities, reflecting on what has been accomplished and examining potential for further inquiry and impact. Our goals are to (a) identify and problematize assessment challenges brought by GenAI through a CSCL lens, (b) examine emerging CSCL theories, pedagogies, and analytics for AI‑enriched assessment, and (c) reflect on assessment practice both as higher‑education instructors and CSCL/learning sciences researchers. We seek to synergize efforts from workshop participants to build collective knowledge, create networks, to address these challenges and to strengthen CSCL’s impact. Theoretical background and themes Theoretical perspective. Since its emergence in the 1990s, CSCL has reconceptualized learning from individual knowledge acquisition to co‑construction of knowledge (Ludvigsen & Steier, 2019). Current concerns about students copying AI‑generated work reflect a continued reliance on surface‑level, transmission‑based conceptions of learning and assessment. Using a CSCL lens, Gen AI use in homework need not be prohibited; instead, it should be scaffolded to support agency, co‑construction, and shared regulation (Järvela, et al., 2023). The knowledge- building model posits collaboration as collective work on continually improvable ideas (Chan & van Aalst, 2018; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014). Similarly, AI‑human collaboration can be conceptualized as iterative idea improvement rather than task completion. We need to shift from policing to scaffolding students to leverage AI as a dialogic partner, using AI‑generated transcripts as evidence for learning and collaboration. CSCL knowledge‑building perspectives could provide a theoretical foundation for unraveling the nature of AI‑human collaboration while enriching CSCL theories in AI age. Design‑pedagogy‑technology perspective. CSCL offers powerful approaches for aligning assessment, learning, and collaboration. Research in assessment has shown that assessment can be understood as assessment of learning (evaluating completed work), for learning (supporting improvement), and as learning (making thinking visible) (Wiliam, 2017). Beyond assessing completed work, CSCL approaches—argumentation, collaborative problem‑solving, knowledge building, and maker work, etc.—provide rich opportunities for formative assessment that support collaboration and complement traditional exams/papers. Assessing group interaction and quality of talk, increasingly supported by AI (Hu et al., 2022), offers important indicators of learning. Reflective assessment enables the assessment of collaboration while also scaffolding interaction and idea development (Yang et al., 2024; van Aalst & Chan, 2007), and this could now be enriched with AI. In this way, AI becomes part of an assessment ecology that supports collaborative learning rather than merely reproducing assignment products. Analytics perspective. Contemporary CSCL analytics research now makes it feasible to assess processes beyond easily replicable products. AI‑enhanced collaborative analytics can trace participation, interactions, and revisions through log data, revealing whether students are engaging in meaningful knowledge construction or simply copying outputs (Ouyang et al., 2023). These process‑level data can be fed back to teachers and learners through dashboards to support monitoring, reflection, and improvement. CSCL researchers are well-positioned to design AI-enriched analytics that make collaboration processes and idea development—previously invisible— now visible (Ba et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2022). This process‑focused view emphasizes ongoing work tracing student engagement and activity rather than post‑hoc grading through concurrent, embedded, and transformative assessment. Such analytics assess not only what students produce but how they collaborate—with AI and with one another—to co-construct and to build knowledge. Issues for Discussion: This workshop provides a platform for participants to share ideas as we inquire into how CSCL could address challenges of assessment for new opportunities in the AI era. Grounded in theory, design, and analytics and ecological-ethical considerations, several areas of inquiry include: ● Focus of assessment and expanding theories. Assessment needs to shift from evaluating products to processes–examining how people learn and collaborate with AI. Emerging research on human–AI collaboration highlights cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and socio-emotional processes, yet more work is needed—for example, on how students take agency and engage in dialogue with AI when tackling assessments to advance learning. Questions also arise about what knowledge, skills, domain-specific competencies, and collaboration processes should be assessed in AI-mediated assessment -- How can AI’s roles shift from merely providing content to supporting co-construction, regulation, and reflection? These shifts call for expanding CSCL theoretical perspectives and engaging with related fields on assessment. Continued inquiry is needed to extend CSCL frameworks to better capture the complexities of learning and collaboration in AI-mediated assessment. ● Collaboration and AI-assessment designs. Building on CSCL designs, researchers can work on productive assessment tasks to replace traditional ones easily emulated by AI and designing AI-enriched collaborative environments. Questions include what we are assessing, what the assessment activity involves, and what resources—peers, AI, and technology—are required. Reflective assessment can prompt students to reflect on their work with AI for ongoing improvement. As well, automatic assessment features can provide teachers with timely information to assess student engagement and to make “on-the-fly” decisions about what support is needed. Design experiments conducted on AI-assessment designs while examining the emerging human-AI collaboration process would help advance both research and practice.. ● Examining AI-supported multi-modal data analysis. Collaborative analytics, combined with AI, can play a central role in assessing learning-collaboration processes via multi-modal data analyses. These could include automatic scoring and annotating student texts and conversations, applying expert-designed rubrics for evaluation, and identifying emerging patterns of behaviors. Information shown in dashboards can support teacher assessment and promote students’ reflection on ongoing work. These analyses open the door to assessing human–AI interactions and designing assessment tasks that capture these dynamics. How these tools and analytics can enhance assessment validity, scalable analysis, providing meaningful insights into collaborative learning processes are important questions. ● Equity and diversity issues. The advent of AI in assessment raises important questions about equity and diversity. AI use may widen existing gaps if students have unequal access to technology, differing levels of guidance, or varying digital literacy. AI technology itself can be biased due to an imbalance in data availability. At the same time, well-scaffolded AI use and mindfully-designed AI tools have the potential to narrow disparities by providing feedback and more accessible pathways for demonstrating student understanding. We need to consider how assessment design and practices can ensure fairness, how AI- based tools can be designed to reduce inequities, and what forms of support learners need to participate equitably in AI-mediated assessment environments. ● Research–practice integration. CSCL-AI assessment for impact involves research-practice synergy developing practical tools and strategies that teachers can use. This involves understanding teachers’ needs and communicating complex findings in accessible, actionable forms. Inquiry such as interviews with teachers about their successful experiences with AI-informed collaboration and assessment could enrich the integration. Supporting higher-education teachers in adopting new views of assessment, collaboration, and AI use—and aligning CSCL research with classroom realities—remain to be investigated. ● Privacy, ethics, and limitations. AI‑supported assessment raises concerns about data privacy, ethical use, and system limitations. Collecting process data—such as interaction logs or conversational traces—requires careful attention to consent, transparency, and responsible data use. Ethical challenges include helping students use AI responsibly, preventing misuse of analytics, addressing bias in AI‑generated judgments, and ensuring students are not harmed by algorithmic errors. Ongoing scrutiny of AI limitations is needed to ensure new CSCL-AI assessment practices remain trustworthy, fair, and beneficial. ● Engagement with the public. The rise of generative AI has sparked widespread public debate, offering CSCL researchers opportunities to engage broader audiences. Public engagement involves helping students, parents, policymakers, and other stakeholders understand the challenges and opportunities AI brings to assessment. By clarifying misconceptions, sharing evidence, success stories, and highlighting responsible uses, CSCL researchers can contribute to more informed public discourse. Outline of planned activities (half-day workshop) Before the workshop: Participants will complete a short survey (a) identifying their research interests in CSCL, assessment, and generative AI, (b) sharing examples of how they have used generative AI in classroom- assessment contexts; and c) proposing key questions for workshop discussion. D uring the workshop: The workshop will be structured to maximize sharing, exchange & knowledge building. • Introduction. Organizers introduce aims and expected outcomes, followed with participant introduction. • Invited panel discussion. 3-4 researchers will be invited to give brief presentations that expand on key themes, also informed by participants’ pre-workshop submissions. • Breakouts and group discussion o Connecting and sharing. In rotating dyads, participants share the big idea or challenge they bring to the workshop, as well as what they hope to gain and contribute. Each person speaks and responds before moving to a new partner. o Knowledge sharing and building: In groups of four, participants rotate and discuss an issue or idea related to their work, focusing on opportunities to develop their research, pursue interdisciplinary collaboration, and take action related to key themes. AI tools could be used to stimulate and help summarize the discussion; each group shares one standout idea from their discussion (online participants will be supported with online collaboration tools) • Closing. Synthesis of what we have learned and reflection on potential actions, including proposed activities on publication, projects, media writing, networking, and community building After the workshop: Participants will form a Google group for communication connecting with CSCL committee /junior researchers and panel discussion planned coming year, opening to CSCL and learning sciences researchers. Expected outcomes and contribution The anticipated outcomes include workshop materials, publication of a paper, collaborative plans for projects and papers; and a Google group for communication for participants and interested ISLS members. Participation requirements Participation requires completing the survey on assessment, CSCL, and generative AI. The survey collects participants’ experience with CSCL and assessment to be shared during the workshop to enrich dialogue. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past (e.g., CSCL or ICLS) This workshop is distinctive in addressing the assessment challenges facing higher education with the rise of generative AI. There could be similar events on CSCL multi-modal analytics and generative AI but few synergizing research and practice for broadening CSCL visions for impacts in assessment in Gen AI era. Facilities and equipment required We will use the conference’s communication platform for remote participants (e.g., Zoom), possibly including other tools, such as Miro (https://miro.com/login/) or Padlet (https://padlet.com/) to support online collaboration.. For on-site participants, internet access, projectors, and a room large enough to accommodate breakout spaces for group discussions are required. Minimal and maximum number of participants We aim for 15 and 25 participants, with a balanced mix of in-person and remote participants, along with the organizing team and invited panelists. Draft call for participation About the Workshop: We invite researchers, graduate students, and practitioners to join this workshop to explore the roles of CSCL in advancing AI-supported assessment. With the rapid rise of generative AI, higher education faces urgent assessment challenges. We propose CSCL offers powerful lenses and tools for rethinking assessment challenges and how learning and collaboration can be assessed in AI‑rich environments. This workshop provides a venue for sharing research, practices, and emerging ideas and future trends on AI‑enriched assessment, including the role of AI as a collaborative partner for knowledge building, process‑focused assessment, assessment design, multi-modal analytics, equity-ethics issues, teacher-researcher collaboration, and public engagement. Together, we will identify ways to address current challenges, examine theories and designs for CSCL-AI enriched approaches, build collective knowledge and reflect on implications for our roles as CSCL researchers and educators. Participants will engage in reflective inquiry, interactive discussions, and community building to reconceptualize assessment and to develop future collaborations on CSCL research for impact. papers.title: Advancing a Learning Sciences Approach to Quantum Information Science in K-12
papers.authors: Raquel Coelho
papers.abstract: My research examines learning in complex, rapidly evolving technological domains, particularly quantum information science. Bridging multiple theoretical perspectives, I am currently pursuing two directions: designing learning environments that make ultra-complex STEM accessible to K-12 learners; and theorizing quantum computational thinking to identify concepts, practices, and perspectives that distinguish quantum from classical reasoning. Research agenda and theoretical framing In my research, I am committed to understanding how emerging technologies shape and support learning. I pursue this understanding both via conceptual inquiry and via the design of learning environments that help learners navigate complex, rapidly evolving domains. While some of my previous (e.g., Coelho & McCollum, 2025) and ongoing work involves empirical investigations using AI and NLP technologies to support teaching and learning across K-12 and post-secondary contexts (e.g., Coelho et al., 2025a), this submission focuses on my research in K-12 quantum information science (QIS). My scholarship is primarily grounded in learning sciences traditions that view learning as situated and mediated by material and social interactions (e.g., Cole, 1998; Moll et al., 2006; Pea, 1985, 1993a, 1993b; Rogoff, 2003). I adopt an integrationist stance (Danish & Gresalfi, 2018), deliberately examining learning across one or more interrelated planes (Rogoff, 2008), while critically attending to the analytic affordances and limitations of this approach and maintaining a commitment to understanding the dynamic interplay among learners, social interactions, and context. I also draw on complementary perspectives that have traditionally emphasized the individual – such as constructivism (Kafai, 2012; Papert & Harel, 1991; Wilensky, 2020) – and cognitive sciences (e.g., Bandura, 2010) as generative for understanding and supporting meaning-making, agency, and motivation. I utilize these complementary perspectives to inform my conceptual and empirical contributions to K-12 quantum information science education as described in the subsequent sections. Thereafter, I discuss future directions centered on studying and designing for quantum computational thinking. Current work When I began reviewing the literature on K-12 quantum information science education (Coelho et al., 2025b), I was surprised to find that learning sciences researchers, who have spent decades studying how students understand complex scientific concepts, were almost entirely absent from the conversations. This absence seemed particularly striking given that learning quantum information science requires learners to grapple with ideas that defy classical intuition and mathematical formalisms that create barriers to accessibility even at the college level, let alone in K- 12 settings. These are precisely the kinds of challenges that learning sciences researchers have developed expertise in addressing: making complex, abstract concepts accessible through appropriate representational tools, scaffolding, and cultural practices that support new ways of thinking. And just as this expertise is most needed, national initiatives are pushing for quantum education to begin in middle and high school (NSF, 2020). While computer science and physics education researchers (e.g., Franklin et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2022) have begun important work in this space, the conversations have yet to substantially engage with learning sciences frameworks and methods that could complement and extend these disciplinary efforts. Our review also showed that both theoretical grounding and design conjectures in K-12 QIS education research remain limited. Many initiatives simply ask, “Does it work?” in a Thomas Edison exploratory framework (Stokes, 2011), without interrogating why or under what conditions learning occurs, risking innovations that engage learners but do not reliably support deep understanding. My position paper (Coelho et al., 2025d) argues for a bidirectional opportunity that neither field has fully recognized. QIS education could leverage learning sciences expertise in design-based research to iteratively develop quantum learning environments. This includes principled approaches for creating new representational infrastructures (Wilensky, 2020) that make quantum phenomena accessible while preserving mathematical integrity, as well as participation structures that allow learners to collectively make sense of quantum phenomena, negotiate meaning through shared representations, and transform their participation in disciplinary practices (Lemke, 2001; Pea, 1992; Rogoff et al., 1995). But equally important, and perhaps more provocative, is what q uantum information science offers the learning sciences: a domain that pushes us to reconsider our theories of conceptual change, representation, and learning at the boundaries of human intuition. To put these conceptual arguments into practice, my recent empirical work (Coelho et al., 2025c) investigates how collaborative game making (Fields & Kafai, 2018) leveraging distributed expertise (Pea, 1993) can support students in developing initial mental models of quantum information science concepts and practice while cultivating curiosity, confidence, and identity – early pathways toward a “competent outsider” stance (Sandoval et al., 2025). We found that designing quantum-themed board games created accessible entry points supporting participation without requiring advanced formalism, though supplementary social and material support will also be incorporated in future iterations of the work. Throughout this process, groups mobilized diverse expertise and resources to materialize quantum ideas, illustrating how even quantum-adjacent activities can drive motivation, sensemaking, and participation in ultra-complex STEM domains. Future work Building on my prior work in K-12 quantum information science education, I have begun to articulate a tentative framework for quantum computational thinking (QCT), extending classical computational thinking to the distinct concepts, practices, and perspectives of quantum information science, while attending to the ethical, societal, and justice-related dimensions of access to quantum technologies (Coelho et al., 2025e). This exploration identifies key concepts (e.g., randomness, interference, superposition), practices (e.g., designing probabilistic algorithms, leveraging amplitude amplification), and perspectives (e.g., understanding computation as materially grounded, designing under indeterminacy) that distinguish QCT from classical computational reasoning, while also emphasizing equitable participation and the social and ethical stakes of access to quantum technologies. Conceptually, this work considers how engagement with QCT might prompt learners to develop non-classical intuitions, reason under uncertainty, and approach computation, abstraction, and scientific problem-solving in fundamentally new ways. Looking forward, my K-12 research agenda focuses on two interrelated directions. First, inspired by the STEM novice/expert research literature (Bransford et al., 2000; Erickson et al., 2006) and Science-Technology- Studies investigations of laboratory life (e.g., Latour, 2005; Latour & Woolgar, 1986), I aim to ground a QCT framework in empirical studies of how quantum information scientists think and work, examining the concepts they use, the practices they enact, and the perspectives they bring to reasoning with quantum phenomena and technologies. Second, I plan to build on these insights by designing and iteratively refining K-12 learning environments that scaffold engagement with QCT, leveraging new representational infrastructures and collaborative practices that invite students into developmentally appropriate, quantum-adjacent forms of authentic inquiry. Such activities may include designing games, music, or visualizations that incorporate principles like amplitude amplification or probabilistic reasoning, enabling learners to make abstract quantum ideas tangible, expressive, and personally meaningful. While practical quantum computers remain on the horizon, progress toward them is uncertain and uneven (Eisert & Preskill, 2025). They are not expected to replace classical systems; instead, future systems will likely integrate both paradigms (Preskill, 2018). The field is already shaped by substantial financial investment to address the enormous hardware challenges. Yet an even greater obstacle lies in identifying problems for which quantum approaches provide decisive advantages, beyond those canonical examples discovered decades ago. How we approach quantum reasoning and learning today will influence not only who gets to participate in shaping this emerging field, but also what kinds of problems we even recognize as solvable. The learning sciences contribution, then, is not auxiliary to quantum computing’s development; rather, it is central to its realization. References Bandura, A. (2010). papers.title: AI-Enhanced Sociocultural, Multimodal Approaches for Equitable Collaborative Learning: Learning, Power, and Multimodality
papers.authors: Hakeoung Hannah Lee
papers.abstract: My research lies at the intersection of the learning sciences, learning analytics, and Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics education, and centers on making collaborative learning more equitable for K–12 learners, particularly multilingual, multicultural, and marginalized youth. Across three interconnected lines of inquiry, I position myself as a scholar who bridges the learning sciences and learning analytics, advancing theoretically grounded, situated, and equity-oriented approaches to illuminate the complexity of collaborative learning at multiple scales.

papers.title: Visualizing Justice: Arts-Based Inquiry in Community-Engaged Climate Education
papers.authors: Rachel Sherwin
papers.abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. Dr. Wise holds a Ph.D. in Learning Sciences and M.S. in Instructional Systems Technology from Indiana University, as well as a B.S. in Chemistry from Yale University, was previously a Professor of Learning Sciences and Educational Technology and Director of the Learning Analytics Research Network (LEARN) at New York University and has worked in industry, with non-profits, and in classrooms across the Americas. https://tinyurl.com/alyssawisescholar https://peabody.vanderbilt.edu/bio/?pid=alyssa-wise https://lab.vanderbilt.edu/live https://www.linkedin.com/in/alyssawise

papers.title: Learning About and Against Generative AI Through Mapping Generative AI’s Ecologies and Developing a Luddite Praxis
papers.authors: Charles Logan
papers.abstract: In this paper, I respond to recent conversations in the learning sciences about how the field might develop research with  generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Rather than a narrow focus on what we might do with  GenAI, I argue that learning scientists should expand our approaches to consider ways to research and learn  about and against GenAI. While AI literacy is a common framework for helping people learn with and about artificial intelligence, a literacy framework can struggle to contend with AI’s opaque systems and is vulnerable to hegemonic influences. I suggest an alternative: mapping ecologies of GenAI and its social, technical, and political- economic relations. Finally, I argue that learning scientists can draw inspiration from the Luddites, 19th- century English clothworkers who destroyed machines to defend their craft and dignity, to develop a Luddite praxis that combines mapping ecologies of GenAI with collective interventions against unjust AI systems. Generative AI and the future of the learning sciences The lecture hall was so crowded that people sat on the floor. Some ISLS 2023 conference attendees had to stand, ringing the room. A few people, I noticed, craned their necks, trying to listen from their place in the hallway. Other people joined the live stream from more comfortable locations. All of us had gathered physically or virtually into John Molson 2.210 for the special session, “The new generation of AI: Opportunities for research and the role of ISLS”. We listened to the panelists offer their persp ectives on how our field might respond to the rapid growth of generative AI. Meanwhile, on a shared digital document, audience members replied to two prompts: 1) What affordances does generative AI create for learning and instruction? 2) How can we, as ISLS researchers, develop an agenda on research with generative AI? Months later, I am still reflecting on those questions and their underlying assumptions that the learning sciences should embrace generative AI. For instance, the first question focuses strictly on the technology’s affordances. What about its limitations? The often dire consequences for people and planet? The second question lacks a similar skepticism. Instead of only asking how the learning sciences might research with  chatbots like ChatGPT, what possibilities are opened when we frame the question as resea rching about and even against generative AI? Scholars outside the learning sciences have been vocal critics of Large Language Models (Bender et al., 2021), and many of these scholars have increasingly warned the public about individuals and companies selling AI hype that draws attention away from  the technology’s immediate impacts in favor of doomsday narratives that harden existing power structures (Bender & Hanna, 2023). The learning sciences has pivotal roles to play in how people understand and use (or refuse to use) GenAI. Perhaps an important initial step would be to ask a new question: What might be required for a more heterogeneous approach to generative AI, one that makes space for learning with, about, and against? In this paper, I make a theoretically grounded conceptual argument for mapping platform ecologies when learning about and against generative AI. Platforms are the infrastructures on which applications are constructed as well as digital spaces where people socialize and conduct economic exchange (Nichols et al., 2022). Platform ecologies are constituted of the intertwined relationships between three dimensions of a platform: social, technical, and political-economic (van Dijck, 2013). GenAI includes Large Language Models (e.g. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini) and Large Image Models (e.g. OpenAI’s DALL -E and Stability AI’s Stable Diffusion) pre - trained on enormous amounts of data scraped from the internet. However, conceiving of GenAI only as a set of tools leaves untroubled the often harmful systems undergirding the advanced technology. In the argument that follows, I will explain that while an AI literacy framework is a more common approach for helping people learn with and about generative AI, it may lack the necessary attributes for “expansive and insurgent ways of learning, being, and acting” (Warren et al., 2020, p. 278) that attends to generative AI’s distributed, often obscured social, technical, and political-economic relations. And in the spirit of insurgency, I will outline what learning scientists might gain from developing a Luddite praxis and its possibilities in the struggle against unjust AI systems. Tracing the emergence of AI literacy and its vulnerabilities AI literacy appears to be having a moment. The popular press offers explainers of the term (Klein, 2023), largely as a consequence of the rapid growth of chatbots and other Gen AI. The push for increased AI literacy is also 362 comi ng from powerful actors in education policy. For example, the non- profit Digital Promise provided funding to the U.S. Department of Education’s Office of Educational Technology and its policy report, “Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning: Insights and Recommendations”. According to Digital Promise, “AI literacy is essential for traversing an increasingly digital society” (Shah, 2023). Describing the history of AI literacy and its different definitions helps to illustrate the u nderlying ideological assumptions about the term and to what ends developing AI literacy may be put. According to Southworth et al. (2023), the term AI literacy  was first used by Konishi (2015)  in a series of posts about priorities for the Japanese economy. In Konishi’s formulation, AI literacy is concerned with identifying new situations for applying AI, focusing on monetizing often very personal artifacts. For example, AI literacy may involve “ record[ing] your mother’s recipe as digitized text. When a cooking robot becomes reality in the future, having the data for one recipe could lead to a new business  of reproducing home cooked meals” (para. 5); people should also “constantly examine whether the information we possess has the potential of generating high value added,” and we should “be emotionally prepared to let go of tasks that AI can perform in our place” (para. 5). Here AI literacy is intertwined with a broader narrative about AI’s inevitability and its promise of individual economic success (if only we can move beyond our doubt and trust the technology and its makers). Absent, however, is a consideration of the ethical and relational implications involved in handing over to Big Tech a family recipe passed down from generation to generation. Another early articulation of AI literacy emphasizes its role in individual economic gain. According to Laupichler et al. (2022), the first appearance of AI literacy  in a peer-reviewed publication was Kandelhofer et al. (2016), who wrote, “AI literacy: It allows people to understand the techniques and concepts behind AI products and services instead of just learning how to use certain technologies or current applications” (p. 2). Again, it’s important to ask to what ends the authors envision AI literacy and its attending technical and conceptual knowledge are working towards. Like Konishi (2015), Kandelhofer et al. (2016) argue the need for AI literacy is predominantly driven by speculative economic trends; they state, “[J]obs will largely be related to AI as it will be the basis of the products where our future wealth will be built on (smart production, internet of things, autonomous driving, robotics . . . )” (p. 1). Such assured prognostication is troubling–and, as it turns out, wrong. Amazon lost $10 billion on Alexa, its AI voice assistant, in 2022 (Amadeo, 2022); autonomous driving cars continue to be a harmful fantasy of the Silicon Valley elite (Marx, 2022). And who, exactly, do the authors include and exclude in their use of “our” in “our wealth”? An AI literacy devoid of power analysis and civic action risks becoming a talking point for Big Tech, and as I discuss shortly, a means for corporations like OpenAI and Google to set the terms of how educators and students think about and use their chatbots. Notably, Kandelhofer et al. (2016) also explicitly root their version of AI literacy in what they refer to as “classic literacy,” or the development of reading and writing skills. Conceiving of AI literacy as analogous to “classic literacy” evokes early theorizations of literacy, known as Great Divide theories ( Higgs et al., forthcoming), that often used a binary of literate versus illiterate to strengthen assertions of white, Western dominance over oral cultures and their literacy practices that did not conform to “civilized” modes of communication. Formulations of AI literacy rarely contend with the multiple meanings of literacy/literacies and how literacy/literacies are sociocultural practices (Street, 1995) enmeshed in struggles for power and legitimacy. Unlike the authors of the early definitions of AI literacy, another influential definition of AI literacy acknowledges that literacy is a contentious term laden with power. In a scoping literature review on AI literacy in higher and adult education conducted by Laupichler et al. (2022), the most cited definition of AI literacy came from Long and Magerko (2020), who draw on Freire (1972) to recognize that literacy is entwined with efforts to repress and liberate. Building on this understanding of literacy as  political, Long and Magerko (2020) go on to define AI literacy as “a set of competencies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace” (p. 2). I want to briefly address two elements of the definition: a focus on AI literacy as an individual skill set; and AI literacy’s emphasis on ethical concerns. The framing of AI literacy as a set of competencies practiced by individuals emerges in part from this version of AI literacy’s roots in a particular form of digital literacy, which Long and Magerko (2020) argue is a requirement for AI literacy. Digital literacy can be characterized as a more prescriptive set of cognitive and behavioral skills for using technology to “find, evaluate, create, and communicate information” (American Library Association, n.d.). Literacy scholars have noted the limited usefulness of a skills-based approach to digital literacy, arguing that such an approach “strains to accommodate the political and economic flows that underwrite contemporary digital activities” (Nichols  & Stornaiuolo, 2019, p. 19). A parallel exists with AI literacy: the competency-based model may not be sufficient for understanding, analyzing, and responding to the  social, technical, and political-economic systems that constitute contemporary GenAI. 363 Even s o, multiple formulations of AI literacy acknowledge the need to address the ethical issues raised by AI (e.g. Miao et al., 2021). Recall that in Long and Magerko’s (2020) influential definition, AI literacy includes the ability to “critically evaluate AI technologies”, a skill further specified through a competency devoted entirely to ethics. To effectively demonstrate this competency, students can analyze how AI deepens existing inequities through applications like predictive policing and job hiring software. Whether in a computer science classroom (Jones & melo, 2021; Vakil, 2018) or an English language arts classroom (Garcia & de Roock, 2021; LeBlanc et al., 2023), justice-oriented education needs to help young people and teachers engage with the ethical dimensions of technology. However, the inclusion of ethics as a core competency of AI literacy must contend with the ways Big Tech has co-opted and sanitized the term “ethics”. AI ethics and safety have been captured by Big Tech firms (Ganesh & Moss, 2022; Rességuier & Rodrigues, 2020; Whittaker , 2021). As a result, a more robust form of ethics committed to centering the lived experiences and expertise of marginalized communities has atrophied into “a practical set of tools and processes, a to-do checklist rather than a moment for critical reflection on power itself” (Ganesh & Moss, 2022, p. 6). Does this cynical, hollowed out version of ethics mean AI literacy should be abandoned? Not necessarily. But proponents of responding to the rapid growth of Gen AI with AI literacy curricula must attend to the ways Big Tech actively shapes the very definition of AI literacy by exercising control over one of its most crucial elements: ethics. Indeed, when we see Common Sense Education publish an AI literacy curriculum  for grades 6 -12 (Common Sense Education, n.d.), we must consider how its parent company Common Sense Media’s partnership with OpenAI (Common Sense Media, 2024) may be shaping how GenAI is framed in the  lesson plans. An AI literacy that fails to examine how Big Tech influences students, educators, and administrators allows corporations to exert a form of soft power through embedding preferred versions of digital literacy that lack analyses of power (Pangrazio & Sefton-Green, 2023). For the learning sciences to continue our commitment to developing learning environments that embrace people’s inherent dignity and agency (Espinoza et al., 2020), we must be explicit about what we mean by AI literacy and be clear-eyed about AI literacy’s possibilities and liabilities. Mapping the ecologies of generative AI and its relations To make explicit the ways AI and issues of power are enmeshed, scholars have argued for a need to develop critical AI literacy (Bali, 2023; Goodlad & Stoerger, 2023). Like critical turns in other forms of literacy (e.g. critical literacy and critical digital literacy), critical AI literacy practices assist people in analyzing how  power operates in ways tangible and less so, and in the case of generative AI, that includes issues related to bias, privacy, misinformation, and the environment. Recently, scholars have questioned the suitability of a literacy framework for analyzing digital platforms (Nichols et al., 2022). Using a literacy lens may be appropriate for understanding different representational forms like an Instagram story or a TikTok video; a literacy lens may also be helpful for analyzing the social practices, connections, and communities that grow as a result of engaging with and through platforms (Ito et al., 2013). But platforms are more than memes and affinity groups. Platforms  are composed of other social dimensions, such as targeted ads made possible by surveillance; technical dimensions such as algorithms trained on limited data sets that reinforce inequities; and political- economic dimensions such as business models that permit the platforms’ owners to sell users’ data to third parties (Nichols & Garcia, 2022) . Therefore, the traditional assemblage of critical digital literacy may not be sufficient for addressing the often opaque social, technical, and political- economic systems undergirding platforms (Nichols & LeBlanc, 2020). By extension, AI literacy, whether critical or not, may also be an insufficient framework for analyzing and responding to GenAI platforms like Google’s Gemini or OpenAI’s DALL-E. Instead, as Nichols et al. (2022) argue, the “familiar critical digital literacy tactics may need to be augmented or reimagined in a media ecosystem where algorithmic rationality is being deployed to foreclose horizons of political possibility” (p. 346). Mapping a platform’s ecologies in order to intervene in its social, technical,  and political- economic relations is one such alternative. As Crawford (2021) argues, “A topographical approach [to AI] offers different perspectives and scales, beyond the abstract promises of artificial intelligence or the latest machine learning models” (p. 11), making possible a deeper understanding of the interconnected landscapes of generative AI. A short example examining OpenAI’s ChatGPT allows a contrast between a literacy framework and an ecological framework. Drawing on Long and Magerko’s (2020) popular definition and competency model, learning scientists might design educational settings and/o r curricula to help educators and their students strengthen their AI literacy by analyzing the outputs of ChatGPT. OpenAI readily admits its chatbot produces false information and contains bias (OpenAI, n.d.). Long and Magerko (2020)’s AI literacy framework includes 16 competencies, and at least two are useful here: describing AI’s strengths and weaknesses; and investigating the human role in AI. Both direct a closer examination of how the chatbot’s social and technical relations combine to produce incorrect outputs. Working with an AI literacy framework to help educators and youth analyze the 364 origi ns of ChatGPT’s biases is helpful. And yet it’s worth asking: what does the literacy framework leave uncharted? An ecological framework that begins to map some of ChatGPT’s social, technical, and political - economic relations helps to illustrate other essential landscapes of the generative AI platform. For instance, ChatGPT’s social relations includes the company’s leadership. OpenAI’s CEO is Sam Altman, whose ideological commitments are influenced by longtermism (Olson, 2023) and its legacy of eugenics (Torres, 2023). Mapping the ideologies of the powerful people releasing GenAI into (and onto) the world raises questions about how those ideologies shape the technologies and whether we should be institutionalizing GenAI platforms through lucrative, long-term contracts that further concentrate power. Attending to these efforts at embedding GenAI platforms and their often damaging ideologies –and related attempts to privatize public education through venture capitalism (Komljenovic et al., 2023) and the Googlization of education worldwide (Kerssens et al., 2023)–is essential work for the learning sciences if, as the conference theme urges, we are to be agents of positive change. Perhaps one of the most important affordances of an ecological framework is its mapping of generative AI’s political-economic relations. AI literacy helps people “[r]ecognize that humans play an important role in programming, choosing models, and fine -tuning AI systems” (Long & Magerko, 2020, p. 6); it’s a necessary competency, even if it adopts a seemingly politically neutral stance towards labor. An ecological framework situates that human labor in a global network of ghost work (Gray & Suri, 2019), exposing the ways Silicon Valley technology firms depend on often harmful, low -wage work on a planetary scale. This work is not only “important”; it’s damaging and exploitative. In the case of ChatGPT, OpenAI contracted with a third- party company to hire Kenyan workers to train the model used for the chatbot. Workers  annotated violent, grotesque text for little pay; many workers were left traumatized and with few resources to heal (Perrigo, 2023). Such violent extraction and indifference to human suffering is characteristic of the AI Empire and its “heteropatriarchal, colonial, racist, white supremacist, and capitalist oppression” (Tacheva & Ramasubramanian, 2023, p. 10). Big Tech’s business and ownership models are another dimension made visible through mapping the ecologies of generative AI’s relations. Educational technology companies are rolling out GenAI tools, many of which rely on OpenAI’s GPT-3 and its more recent updates. Khan Academy recently announced its own chatbot, Khanmigo. Schools are piloting the chatbot, including several in Newark, New Jersey. And while the pilot phase is free, the distric t will eventually need to pay $70 per student to license Khanmigo (Singer, 2023). Khan Academy’s business model relies on a rentier -rentee relation with schools, a relation that allows Khan Academy and OpenAI to further consolidate power through various forms, from the monetary gains obtained through licensure fees to the extraction and monetization of teachers’ and students’ data (Komljenovic, 2021). Notably, the Newark schools piloting Khanmigo–a chatbot without empirical research supporting its ability to aid teaching and learning–serve nondominant students (Singer, 2023). Khanmigo must therefore be understood as yet another teaching machine foisted upon nondominant communities by outsiders with mixed intentions. In the mid- 20th century, B. F. Skinner attempted to enroll Black students in Harlem schools as test subjects to see whether or not his teaching machine could help them learn to read (Watters, 2021). While he failed, Sal Khan and his company’s problematic business and ownership model appears to be gaining traction. Generative AI’s extractions are not limited to human beings. Our planet is also a source of extraction for GenAI. OpenAI used coal and natural gas to power the computing used to train its GPT -3 LLM, which resulted in the release of 500 metric tons of carbon or driving the average gasoline -powered car one million miles (Luccioni, 2023). Big Tech companies like Microsoft and Google acknowledge they are using more and more water to cool the servers needed to maintain their LLMs and other Gen AI tools (O’Brien &  Fingerhut, 2023). Emerging research estimates that OpenAI’s ChatGPT requires 16 ounces of water to respond to 5 to 50 prompts (O’Brien & Fingerhut, 2023). The water used to make generative AI possible is making life increasingly impossible for humans and more than humans living close to the data centers that contain the whirring servers (Hao, 2024). As water is diverted to cool servers, less water is available for residents in places like West Des Moines, Iowa, taxing a water system already at risk thanks to ongoing droughts. One organizer with the Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement put the problem like this: “‘ChatGPT is not a necessity for human life, and yet we are literally taking water to feed a computer’ ” (Adralo, 2023, para. 3). Hogan (2024) sums up the  crisis succinctly: “AI is a hot mess.” Climate change is one of the most urgent problems facing humanity. An ecological approach to mapping generative AI’s relations helps people to understand the web of connections between a dwindling water table in Carlisle, Iowa, and a blank ChatGPT interface on a laptop in Buffalo, New York. Mapping the ecologies of generative AI platforms and their relations does not guarantee such an approach will be beyond Big Tech’s influence. Creating maps and atlases has always been a subjective exercise, one that presents a particular view of the world (Crawford, 2021). The method demands reflexivity and an ongoing commitment to using design practices that deconstruct normative power hierarchies (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). 365 One w ay learning scientists and the people we work alongside can build these just relations is through using a mapping framework to identify points of intervention in order to take action. From maps to movements A map is not only a static image of interconnected environments; it’s also an invitation to action. I have focused on the harms of generative AI, yet mapping the ecologies of generative AI and its social, technical, and political - economic relations is not meant to solely illustrate forms of extraction. As Nichols and Garcia (2022) argue, “The promise of platform studies in education, then, is not to map in detail the vast scope of exploitations encapsulated in networked media but instead to identify where and how these relations might be changed and what role education might play in such transformations” (p. 225). Maps in hand, learning scientists and the diverse groups we work with can identify points of intervention to bring about change. We have historical and contemporary examples to help guide us. First, we can look towards the Luddites. The 19th century English clothworkers did not, contrary to popular belief, oppose technological change. Rather, the clothworkers opposed wealthy factory owners installing machines that automated their craft and impoverished their communities, and when attempts to regulate the mach ines failed in Parliament, the clothworkers embodied the fictional hero Ned Ludd and banded together to smash gig mills and power looms to protect their individual and collective dignity (Merchant, 2023). Like the Luddites, contemporary screenwriters understood the social and political-economic relations between an advanced technology deployed by powerful bosses and the screenwriters’ livelihoods. They went on strike, demanded limited applications of generative AI, and they won. The screenwriters’ new contract dictates that the writers have control over when and how Gen AI platforms are used in their work (Anguiano & Beckett, 2023).  What emerges from these examples is a praxis that couples the need to map and understand the relations of generative AI with a commitment to acting on that knowledge to intervene in unjust systems. Developing a Luddite praxis extends existing calls for learning scientists to join organizers  in bringing about social change (Curnow & Jurow, 2021). To imagine what living a Luddite praxis might look like, consider the learning and coalition-building that could occur to combat the construction of a new data center (Pasek, 2023). In this scenario, students might begin much as I have: by mapping some of the ecologies of generative AI and their relations. Then, after locating their nearest data center, students can begin their inquiry into the center, examining questions such as, “What potential land use, energy, or water conflicts might exist because of the data center?” and “Who benefits from the data center being here? Who loses?” (Pasek, 2023). From there, youth might explore what local groups may be affected by the data center’s construction, from Indigenous peoples on whose lands and waters the data center threatens to neighbors who will be force d to live with the data center’s noise pollution. Alongside and in conjunction with the different coalitions, students can assert their civic leadership through multiple, youth-led actions (Mirra & Garcia, 2017). Here, perhaps, is a role for literacy: as a nested set of practices within an ecological stance towards generative AI that can help, for example, youth construct and analyze a persuasive set of images to include in a fight against Microsoft and a proposed data center. Working in tandem, both approaches combine to make for powerful learning about and against generative AI. A Luddite praxis is counter -hegemonic; its pedagogy is one of “disobedience and dismantling…of refusal and of care” (Watters, 2020, para. 16). In its open embrace of politics and action, a Luddite praxis aligns with the learning sciences and the field’s in creasing acknowledgement that learning is political (McKinney de Royston & Sengupta-Irving, 2019; The Politics of Learning Writing Collective, 2017; Vea et al., 2023). If, as a field, we are to realize the conference theme and the call to “strengthen our own practices leading to human flourishing,” we might design learning experiences that help people to map the ecologies of GenAI and its relations as part of a broader Luddie praxis dedicated to collective action against inequities and towards more just futures. Conclusion The learning sciences has a complicated relationship with artificial intelligence. While the field’s origins appear to have been a deliberate break from artificial intelligence (Hoadley, 2018), recently scholars have argued it’s time to revisit the relationship between the learning sciences and AI (Doroudi, 2023). Importantly, what we mean when we speak of AI has evolved since Roger Shank renamed what was supposed to be an Artificial Intelligence in Education conference into the first International Conferen ce of the Learning Sciences. For some, AI is now a powerful marketing term (Raji, 2023; Whittaker, 2021). AI in education is a methodology for academic research; a potential revenue stream for industry; and political rhetoric wielded by policymakers in the  pursuit of educational reforms (Williamson, 2023). The politicized nature of AI and its multiple definitions demand approaches to learning with, about, and against Gen AI that accounts for the visible and invisible relations that constitute AI systems. 366 As I ’ve argued, mapping the ecologies of generative AI and its social, technical, and political-economic relations is a productive approach to understanding the opaque, distributed landscapes of GenAI. When combined with a Luddite praxis, an ecological approach can support collective intervention and possible transformations of unjust systems. AI literacy may have a more limited role to play because it’s enmeshed with a history that deepens hegemonic conceptions of literacy; struggles to counteract a literacy framework’s focus on representational forms; and suffers from a vulnerability to Big Tech’s preferred versions of self -serving ethics. An ecological approach to generative AI platforms is not the only way for addressing the complex problems posed by Gen AI. However, our maps can bring into focus the connections between a planet warming from the carbon produced by training chatbots and a school -issued laptop warming from entering prompts into an increasingly expensive, proprietary chatbot. The connections laid out before us, we can join together with others to resist, refuse, and reimagine what and for whom generative AI might be put to use. References Amadeo, R. (2022, November 21).
