papers.title: Designing for Expansive Forms of STEAM Disciplinary Engagement
papers.authors: Carrie Tzou, Elizabeth Starks, Veronica Cassone McGowan, Bryan White, Jordan Sherry- Wagner, Symone Gyles, Forrest Bruce, Christa Haverly, Mario Guerra, Megan Bang, Angela Booker, UC San Diego
papers.abstract: Increasingly, calls from within the natural and computational sciences are recognizing the need for more expansive forms of disciplinary theory building and practice to connect social theories in the study of natural systems. Within science education and s cience teacher education, there is an increasing recognition of the need for expansive forms science teaching that connect sociopolitical contexts of science with both the professional learning of teachers and the science taught in K12 classrooms. In this symposium, we explore designs for expansive STEAM disciplinary engagement across classroom, professional learning, and informal Indigenous STEAM settings to understand the ways in which work at the edges of disciplines can transform STEAM teaching and learning for educators and students. Rationale and contribution: Understanding STEAM disciplines, learning and learning environments as always deeply connected to sociopolitical contexts (McKinney deRoysten & Sengupta -Irving 2019) allows us to engage with the “ethical entanglements” (Krishnamoorthy & Tolbert, 2022) inherent in doing, being,  and learning in STEAM.  Yet the forms of disciplinary engagement often present in STEM and STEAM learning environments often represent settled knowledge that mutes the dynamic, heterogeneous, anti-colonial commitments driving STEM and STEAM disciplinary work at the edges of the disciplines.  Within science education and science teacher education, there is an increasing recognition of the need for expansive forms science teaching that connect sociopolitical contexts of science with bot h the professional learning of teachers (Madkins & McKinney de Royston, 2019) and the science taught in K12 classrooms (Davis & Schaeffer, 2019; Jones, 2024). Increasingly, calls from within the natural and computational sciences are recognizing the need for more expansive forms of disciplinary theory building and practice to connect social theories in the study of natural systems (Schell, et al, 2020; Duncan, et al, 2024). For example, Schell, et al’s review (2020) argued that understanding key socio -ecological factors related to, for example, urban heat islands, tree canopy cover and biodiversity, and speciation needs to be critically tied to histories of places that include redlining and racial and class segregation (Schell, et al, 2020). Ongoing debates within ecology around the inadequacy of Darwin’s sexual selection theory to account for the abundance of same-sex behavior in the natural world have highlighted need for more expansive forms of studying and teaching about gender/sex in the natural world that move the field towards multiplicities and fluidities of gender and biological sex (Roughgarden, 2013).  In the midst of disinformation campaigns, policing of black and brown bodies using surveillance technologies, and proliferation of digital tools for anything from voice recognition to hiring to grocery delivery, scholars working in AI and design of technology and computing systems are increasingly foregrounding the connection between societal structures that uphold white supremacy and settler colonialism and the algorithms that affect our daily lives (Benjamin, 2019). At the same time, a new report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM): Equity in K -12 STEM Education: Framing Decisions for the Future  (NASEM, 2024), calls for a clearer articulation of the kinds of powered decision- making that work towards particular purposes for equitable STEM education. The report presents the field with five “equity frames”, or “conceptions of equity that can be and a re used as rationale for decision -making” (p. 133). These are: (1) reducing gaps between groups, (2) 2487 expanding opportunity and access, (3) embracing heterogeneity in STEM classrooms, (4) learning and using STEM to promote justice, and (5) envisioning sustainable futures through STEM. While all five decision-making frames are important in working towards equity across all levels of educational systems, some may be more present than others. In this symposium, we focus on frames 3- 5 as key decision- making frames for the kinds of expansive designs of disciplinary engagement that we argue for. For example, in reference to Frame 3, embracing heterogeneity in STEM classrooms, the report states that Rather than move toward a ‘single story’ or narrative of disciplines, disciplines are understood as evolving and internally heterogeneous, and as cultural practices for developing and warranting knowledge claims...STEM [is] a cultural and sociopolitical en deavor, situated in time, place, and within networks of power.”  (NASEM, 2024, p.6-12) All these examples (and more) necessitate a re- imagining and de -settling of how we engage all learners (K -12 students and their families, educators, educational leaders, and even scientists) with expansive forms of STEAM disciplines, where the disciplines themselves are re-imagining more just futures of their work. The five studies in this symposium will describe work at the intersection of STEAM disciplinary learning, social theories, and changemaking towards heterogeneous and expansive learning in the disciplines. Across the symposium, the papers will give us visions of  design for expansive STEAM learning across multiple contexts, grade levels, and disciplinary domains. We describe the design for expansive forms of AI and gender affirming biology with practicing educators in papers 1 and 2. Papers 3 and 4 describe designing for  learning in informal Indigenous STEAM programming towards expansive relations with waters and plants. Finally, paper 5 describes expansive modeling practices in a place-based, elementary program. Paper 1: Expansive engineering: Artificial intelligence use and development in education toward justice, sovereignty, and equity Elizabeth Starks, Veronica McGowan, Symone Gyles, Bryan White, Megan Bang, Carrie Tzou Framing and study design We acknowledge our moment in time when artificial intelligence (AI) is an integrated and growing part of our designed world and also acknowledge our responsibility as educators, designers, researchers, learners, and as part of ecosystems, to understand the  powered decisions that have led to current inequities in order to build a more just future. In this paper, we describe the design and implementation of a 3- day professional development series, CS and AI toward Justice, Sovereignty, and Equity .  In this PD series, we build on the work of Indigenous information scientists and computer scientists who have been thinking critically about data sovereignty on cultural and tribal levels, building data systems that reflect sovereignty across scale and access (Lewis, 2020; Hendrix, 2023) We use critical sociotechnical literacy (McGowan & Bell, 2020) as a method for educators to practice equitable approaches to both the use of AI by educators and learners, and teaching of computer science. In the PD series, educators spent time researching their school’s guidelines or standards about AI use and developing their own stances based on their interactions with data and conversations during the professional development. We ask the following questions: (1) How does the professional development series shift educators’ understanding of the intersection between CS/AI and power and historicity? (2) What sense do educators make of sovereignty and how that applies to AI and data systems? Data sources and analysis Participants were from 13 states, in both in and out of school settings, and spanned K-16 contexts, state leadership, and instructional coaches. Data were collected from online professional development recordings (Zoom), digital artifacts created by participants in the sessions, daily exit tickets, and post-interviews with participants. For space purposes, we will focus below on qualitative and quantitative exit ticket data. We used emergent coding and grounded theory (Strauss & Corbin, 1997) to analyze exit ticket data and understand educators’ sensemaking and shifting stances on AI and equity. Findings Exit ticket data show that as they participated in the professional development, educators’ confidence increased in their knowledge around topics related to AI, the social context of new technologies, and their familiarity with their school’s policies and standards on AI. Educators also gained a deeper understanding of the ethical considerations surrounding AI, particularly in relation to data sovereignty, bias, and equity.  The PD also helped educators to expand their understandings of the importance of da ta sovereignty, especially for marginalized and Indigenous communities, as it involves control over one's own data and its use. For example, educators recognized 2488 that respecting cultural data and preventing its misuse by corporations or AI systems are essential for ethical AI practices. This realization led them to consider integrating discussions about data ownership, privacy, and the consequences of corporate control over personal stories and information into their curriculum. Educators' responses also demonstrated their grappling with the bias and equity issues inherent in AI. They described coming to understand that AI is shaped by the data used to build it, oft en reflecting historical and systemic biases particularly harmful to BIPOC communities. At the start of the course, 4/19 respondents stated that they feared AI, and 5/19 said they did not really understand what it was (day 1 exit survey). During the course of the PD, educators began to see AI's broader societal impacts. They described shifting their focus towards ethical AI use, emphasizing the importance of transparency, responsible engagement, and understanding AI's potential to both benefit and harm society, including guiding students to become creators of AI tools rather than just users and fostering critical thinking about the data and algorithms behind AI systems. This deeper awareness marks a significant shift from their previous views, as educators moved towards a more nuanced understanding of AI's complexities and responsibilities in education. They reported that this course highlighted the need for an equity- centered approach to AI, where students are encouraged to question AI’s fairness and how it impacts various communities. Below is an excerpt from exit tickets: Data sovereignty [was a powerful idea I took away from this course]. I had no sense of what this term really meant prior to the session, but now I'm thinking about it in many settings/contexts. Integration [was another]. This was already on my radar, but t his learning emphasized the importance of integrating CS into and across all content areas in meaningful ways. Bias [is a third powerful idea I took away from this course].  I have a better sense of what this means in the context of AI and how I can use this to support broader understanding of bias and equity issues with data.  (Educator Exit Ticket, Summer 2024) Many educators had never considered data sovereignty as related to education or been asked to consider their social histories as connected with technologies. Implications and contributions Much of the concern around generative AI in educational settings centers around fears of plagiarism and “cheating” (Lee, et al, 2024). While we acknowledge these concerns, we also position AI (and educators) as situated within larger systems of power, wher e generative AI represents a larger ecosystem of technologies that have the power to reproduce or resist existing societal inequities. For example, by sharing the work of Indigenous technology developers and information scientists who are developing systems that contribute to sovereignty in AI, we not only foreground the presence Indigenous people in STEM, but highlight the importance of Indigenous research and ways of knowing in innovating toward cultural revitalization. In this way, we show how these same technologies can be used toward justice and help educators imagine more hopeful futures. Paper 2: Designing for expansive futures: Sex and gender justice in teacher education Veronica McGowan, Bryan White, Elizabeth Starks, Symone Gyles, Megan Bang, Carrie Tzou Framing and study design Science is a powerful set of knowledge and practices that can be simultaneously liberating and oppressive, as they shape the lived realities of individuals either seen or invisibilized solely through Western scientific theories (Krishnamoorthy & Tolbert, 2022). Understanding the impact of science on people and communities calls for science to address social theories in their work (Graddy -Lovelace, 2017). There is a need to prepare preservice and in-service educators to address the sociopolitical contexts of teaching, learning, and doing science in order to pave pathways for STEM education to contribute to the cultivation of just, sustainable and thriving communities (NASEM, 2024). In this work we describe the design and enactment of an interdisciplinary undergraduate STEM course module entitled Queer Ecologies and Gender Affirming Biology. This module serves as part of a sequence of two “science for elementary teachers” science content courses that center racial justice and gender equity as a part of STEM teaching and learning for educators. These courses take the place of required science content courses typically taken by preservice educators towards completion of their degree pathways. Here we share enactment data from both our pre-service course module and the adapted version of this module for an in-service professional learning series. Each course module in this project was created through co -design with an interdisciplinary tea m of faculty across STEM disciplines, learning scientists, and community experts. 2489 Queer Ecology seeks to disrupt heteronormative projections onto nature and to trouble how cultural dualisms get grafted onto entangled, complex ecosystems (Roughgarden, 2013).The module described in this research engages learners in exploring 1) The social context of sex, gender, sexuality, 2) examination of data from scientific studies of same sex behavior in the natural world, 3) diversity of sex determination in the natural world, social vs. sexual selection,  and 4) examination of data and case studies on the range of mechanisms and hormone signals related to human sex development, gender, and sexuality.  In our work we ask, how can we move away from “single story” dominant disciplinary narratives of sex, gender and sexuality towards more accurate as well as equitable disciplinary ways of knowing that are understood as evolving and internally heterogeneous and encompassing cultural as well as empirical ways of knowing. Data sources and analysis We use framing theory which recognizes how frames are taken up or not depending on powered relationships assumed within interactions (Hand, Penuel, Gutiérrez, 2013; NASEM, 2024) and master narrative theory  which acknowledge how culturally shared stories, beliefs, values that shape thought, decision- making, and behavior (Bradford & Syed, 2019) as theoretical framings for our coding and analysis. Data for this analysis come from a 10-week online professional learning course that met for 1.5 hours/ week for approximately 25 practicing educators across content areas and contexts. The online course was an adapted version of our undergraduate course module, which was co-taught by two instructors with backgrounds in queer ecology and gender-affirming biology. Data include weekly whole group zoom recordings and transcripts, exit ticket reflections, recorded small group discussions, in -class artifacts, and course design artifacts. We conducted emergent coding for themes (Miles, Huberman, Saldaña, 2019), and then used grounded theory to make sense for emergent patterns across data sets (Corbin & Strauss, 2014). Our first level coding includes themes related to two “master narratives” as frames, and second level coding included application of queer ecology theories to understanding how educators were pushing against, making sense of, and/or becoming attuned to master narratives. Third level coding focused on the mechanisms and processes of teaching and learning expansive science. Findings Our findings show that this work made visible to educators the “master narrative” of gender essentialism in science that upholds gender binaries and ideas of fixed biological sex in texts and other teaching and learning materials. As one participant reflected, “The binary language of gender and sex is SO ingrained in my teaching of genetics even though I see the human world as complex, queer and non- binary.” Participants also shared that engaging with data around the diversity of sex, gender, and sexuality in the natural world illuminated aspects of ecology and evolution that were never made visible to them in prior learning contexts (such as their own biology education). For example one participant asked, “why have I never learned this and why aren’t we set  up to teach this?” With raised awareness educators became more attuned to the pervasive language of gender binaries used in science and science standards and curriculum, and surfaced the need for more scientifically accurate materials for teaching about sex diversity in classrooms. As one participant shared, “I can't stomach teaching to a test with the reality of science knowledge being so different.” In this professional series, participants co- designed gender- affirming activities for their own contexts that included engaging students in analysis of expansive data sets and using case studies from humans and other species to support expansive notions of sex, gender, and sexuality. Implications and contributions Our work shows that engaging educators with expansive scientific data was a powerful tool for making settled knowledge visible, and helped move participants to both more inclusive and more accurate framings of the diversity of sex, gender, and sexuality. Engaging with the complexity within and between scientific theories allowed educators insight into the ways in which scientific knowledge evolves over time and opened up opportunities to engage with data-informed gender-affirming teaching and learning to create more just, equitable, and inclusive science teaching and learning environments. Paper 3: Relationality with water as a design ontology Forrest Bruce, Megan Bang Framing and study design This paper will discuss relationality with water as a design ontology in the context of an Indigenous STEAM program (ISTEAM). ISTEAM is a multisite community-based design research (CBDR) project that seeks to build thriving communities, composed of human and more -than-human (MTH) life, through the regeneration of Indigenous land- and water-based systems of education. Through CBDR, ISTEAM engages Indigenous families 2490 and community members to dream and enact educational possibilities for their communities (Bang et al., 2016). One purpose of this study is to further explicate the process by which co- design cultivates iterative processes of dreaming, future making, and proleptic enactments in educational spaces in the here and now with co- designers, youth, and families (Ishimaru et al., 2018; Hall et al., 2020). We analyze the processes of dreaming and enactment in the context of a three year, multisite design arc where In digenous community members designed for water education in each of their respective communities. While there has been significant work to unearth the epistemologies and axiologies embedded in design processes (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016), there remains a need to examine the understandings of reality – the ontologies – that underpin the design of learning environments. We put forth that co- design involves the navigation of multiple ontologies and that the engagement with ontological multiplicity further creates grounds for both ontological and axiological innovations (Bang, 2016). For Indigenous people, designing for learning through Indigenous ontologies means that we engage with lands and waters as co-designers, a process that we call place-based design. The corporeal arrangement of activity is closely tied to the ontological assumptions about humans and their relationship to the natural world (Marin, 2020). This paper seeks to further understand how the corporeal arrangement of co -design creates new ontological grounds for dreaming and enacting thriving socio- ecological futures. In doing so we examine Indigenous community members’ dreams for water education, and how these dreams emerge temporally over the lifecourse of design and spatially across various corporeal arrangements. Data sources and analysis ISTEAM is a three- year, multi-site project that involves multiple streams of audiovisual data that reflect both community specific design as well across community design work. There are a total of 123 co- design sessions included in the data corpus. The design process deliberately engaged in distinct corporeal arrangements ranging from in -person, place -based design work to virtual cross -site sessions. We conduct a longitudinal micro- ethnography (Erickson, 1996)  of microinteractions in the design process ove r time and space. Our first round of analysis focuses on the conceptual ecology in each design meeting with respect to water. The second layer of analysis characterized the different dreams for water and water education that were articulated by co -designers. Once both rounds of codes were complete, we selected “hot spots” in the data that reflected the codes from round 1 and 2 of analysis – places where there are a density of codes – and conducted  interaction analysis for pivotal micro-moments in the desig n process (Jordan & Henderson, 1995). Additionally, we have conducted design interviews where co -designers reflect on their relationship to local waterways and their participation in the last three years of ISTEAM. Using these different data streams, we conducted a spatialized diachronic analysis (Saxe & Esmonde, 2005) that traces how co- designers dreams for water and water education emerged from a series of micro-interactions that take place across multiple spatial configurations involving humans, MTHs, la nds and waters. Findings Though we are continuing to refine our analysis, we have two preliminary findings to share. First, there was a deepening of human- water relations over time. While ontologies of respecting water were present from the beginning, relations with water were often enclosed by colonial, human- centered ontologies. This enclosure was evident in the way that early co -design meetings would sometimes focus on the feasibility of learning along waterways (e.g. safety, logistics, staying dry). Later meetings tended to focus on water pedagogies or ways of enacting relations with water (e.g. water -based practices, songs and stories involving water). We see this turn towards enactment as evidence for the cultivation of kinship ontologies with water over time (Van Horn et al., 2021). In other words, there was a shift from more psychologically distant notions of human- water relationality mediated by coloniality towards more psychologically close discussions of how to be a good relative – how to be kin – to water (Van Horn et al., 2021). Second, physical engagements with nearby waterways through place-based design became a site of engagement for asserting a kinship ontology (Bang, 2016; Todd, 2014). Specifically, canoeing, a central practice to Indigenous lifeways for countless generations, was instrumental for cultivating a kinship ontology. As some co -designers have discussed in their interviews, traversing water on canoes was a corporeal arrangement that opened up new possibilities for enacting human- water relations in a lived way. Implications and contributions This work has important implications for the design and pedagogical practice as it will articulate design principles for creating water -based learning environments that support more ethical human -water relations. Specifically, findings will demonstrate the  role that corporeal arrangements play in establishing ontological grounds for 2491 dreaming and enacting educational possibilities in co -design processes. These findings will contribute to a framework that allows design -based researchers to more deeply understand the implications for the spatial organization of design. A deeper understanding for the spatial implications of design will be beneficial for establishing design processes grounded in relational ontologies in which humans are interconnected with lands and waters. Such design processes are necessary for building systems of educati on that cultivate thriving socio - ecological futures. Paper 4: Each one teach one Mario Guerra, Megan Bang Framing and study design Our planet is currently experiencing unprecedented changes as a result of human actions, yet a significant portion of the population remains unaware or chooses to ignore this reality. The ecosystem and ongoing climate crisis are complex systems—"usually made up of many individuals displaying a variety of behaviors; and yet, they exhibit a predictable pattern as a group (Levy & Wilensky, 2008, p. 2).” Understanding complex systems means grasping the interconnectedness of individual entities and how their interactions lead to the emergence of new, distinct patterns. These emergent patterns wouldn't exist without individual agent -level interactions. Frameworks for understanding these interactions —which can better conceptualize complex ecological systems —are fou nd in many Indigenous communities. As Muller et al. (2019)  conclude, "Indigenous ways of being and worldviews based on connection, reciprocity, and ethical relationships epitomise what is missing in the mainstream doctrine of environmental management" (p. 18). These Indigenous perspectives, with their deep connections to the land and intricate interweaving of place and thought (Watts, 2013) , are thus vital in addressing climate change issues. As Watts (2013) concludes “Thus, habitats and ecosystems are better understood as societies from an Indigenous point of view; meaning that they have ethical structures, inter- species treaties and agreem ents, and further their ability to interpret, understand and implement. Non-human beings are active members of society." From this deep connection to the land emerges what we term a "cultural aggregate"—ideas shaped through iterative learning processes spanning time immemorial. These concepts aggregate a collective understanding of agents and embody teachings about relational responsibility. As a result, ecological decision -making can more ethically incorporate non-human perspectives. Data sources and analysis This paper examines the interaction of Indigenous youth through the ISTEAM program and “Each One Teach One” activity. During this activity, students learned about specific plants and then shared their knowledge with others. Over the 1.5 hour session, we gathered audio and video data from students and facilitators, allowing us to closely observe and analyze how students engaged with Indigenous perspectives and the natural environment. The groups in the activity consisted of between 2 and 5 students, one faci litator, and one plant card with information about their specific focal plant. Of the 8 total groups in the activity, 5 had a student recording the activity through a chest mounted GoPro resulting in a total of 8 hours and 12 minutes of video. In analyzing the data, we first created excerpts from ambulatory sequences as our primary unit for interaction analysis (Hall & Stevens, 2015; Marin, 2020) . After creating excerpts, we analyzed the discourse to characterize the epistemic ecologies with respect to complex systems reasoning within each sequence. More specifically, we examined these sequences for agents or aggregates in student reasoning/activity. Findings The results of this study reveal how Indigenous stories and cultural knowledge shaped students' understanding during the E1T1 activity discussions. Throughout the activity, students engaged with both individual plants (agents) and broader species -level concepts (aggregates) through traditional stories and teachings. The analysis revealed that what we term “cultural aggregates” - knowledge passed down through generations - helped students toggle between agent and aggregate level reasoning while considering complex systems. Closer examination of excerpts with similar ratios of agent and aggregate -level actors unveiled insightful conversations about focal plants, their ecological communities, and humanity's role within the ecosystem. In sum, students readily employed both agent -level thinking (when directly interacting with individual plants) and aggregate -level understanding (through cultural teachings or “cultural aggregate”) while learning about or teaching their focal plants. Implications and contributions The design and implementation of the "Each One Teach One" activity demonstrated how learning with nature, particularly through Indigenous and relational ontologies, fostered complex systems thinking and deeper learning 2492 among participants. Perspective -taking—facilitated through plant cards and storytelling —helped refine the "cultural aggregates" and integrate them into the conversation. These aggregates enabled students to consider the well-being of an entire species. These findings suggest that outdoor learning activities, designed to foster agent - aggregate toggling, can effectively facilitate complex systems thinking among students. By interacting directly with the natural world, students can apply abstract concepts to t angible experiences, thereby deepening their understanding of ecological systems. The use of cultural aggregates presents a promising model for education that fosters deep, multifaceted understanding of ecological systems. By combining perspective -taking, relational ontologies, and outdoor learning, we created a rich learning environment that encouraged students to think critically about their place within the natural world. This approach might not only enhances ecological sensibility but also has the potential to nurture a generation of individuals who are more attuned to the complexities of nature and more inclined towards sustainable practices. Paper 5: Socio-ecological systems modeling: Place-based design for ethical deliberation and change-making with youth and their families Jordan Sherry-Wagner, Christa Haverly, Carrie Tzou, Megan Bang Framing and study design In this conceptual paper we describe an empirically- engaged approach to socio-ecological systems modeling we are continuing to develop through the Learning in Places project. Grounded in the Learning in Places material ecosystem and Field -Based Seasonal St oryline for Transdisciplinary Education, we elevate how the process of model development contributes to desettling normative expectations across multiple dimensions of inquiry, and to generate innovative modeling practices that support imagining and enacting more healthful, sustainable, and just forms of living with the rest of the natural world (Bang et al., 2013) . In our work, these include: contextualizing inquiry within particular places through routine and extended outdoor sensemaking (i.e. wondering walks); grounding models in the noticings, values, histories, and expertise of learners, families, and communities as central to sensemaking with models; and expanding normative epistemic foci of models to also attend to ontological and axiological dimensions of possible decisions in complex socio- ecological systems. Data sources and analysis Drawing on data gathered from our co -design work with educators, youth, and families, this paper describes preliminary analysis of modeling data to develop key dimensions and trace important implications of our approach to modeling with educators. Data sources include socio -ecological systems models co -designed in professional learning sessions with educators over three years and their related whole and small group discussions; reflection ticket results across the PL session; artifacts from classroom implementation of socio -ecological systems models developed with children; and iteratively revised instructional materials to support modeling in classrooms. We analyzed the data over time to understand (a) our own trajectory of understanding the role of modeling for educator and student learning, (b) our own mediation to support educator learning about modeling, (c) educator sensemaking and implementation of modeling practice in learning environments,  and (d) how children engage with this practice over time. Findings Over the course of our engagement with educators and children in socio- scientific modeling, we have come to understand modeling as a sensemaking practice designed to support learners in understanding why, how, and under what conditions socio- ecological phenomena happen the way they do, as well as how place, time, power, and human intervention influence socio- ecological relationships. Used for both individual and collective sensemaking (i.e. ensemble modeling (Learning in Places Collaborative, 2021), our des ign elevates emergent forms of modeling (Lehrer & Schauble, 2005) in which learners build models that represent their collective sensemaking about socio -ecological phenomena and relationships as grounded in their particular field- based experiences. Rather than static and wholly explanatory, these models are designed to be dynamic and ever - changing based on new data and other types of information learned through the investigation of phenomena, discussion with others (i.e. wondering talks) and learning from other sources of media (books, video, etc.). In the recent report on equity in K -12 science education, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Mathematics (NASEM, 2024) defined equity as a process and an outcome. We see the process of creating, revising, and sensemaking with socio- ecological systems models as equitable modeling and pedagogical practice. The equitable outcomes of this practice we recognize as expanded views of who does science and a change in relationships to the discipline of science and with places. We also see equitable outcomes 2493 as young children being given opportunities to attend to complexity, understand out responsibilities within the rest of the natural world, and engage in deeper noticing, wondering, and ethical deliberation in ways that expand and diversify possibilities for life within (and beyond) context of disciplinary learning (Warren et al., 2020). Implications and contributions We understand our approach to modeling as having significant implications for how we imagine possible decisions and approaches to sustainable change -making as connected to particular places. In this way, our approach intervenes in a persistence of de -placed, decontextualized, or abstracted forms of inquiry and representation that can reproduce coloniality and western rationalist approaches to learning and change- making (Vossoughi et al., 2023). Through iterative cycles of model development informed by routine learning experiences within particular outdoor places, our approach to modeling supports expanded construction of agency whereby places, lands, waters, and more- than-humans are understood as active mediators of complex socio- ecological sensemaking (McDaid Barry et al., 2023). Situated in particular places aimed at informing possible courses of action we could take, such models support psychologically close construals of family, self, and community as existing as a part of the rest of the natural world. In Learning in Places, we see an opportunity to expand modeling practices to include other forms of representations (such as artistic representations of socio- ecological systems) that hold deep potential for ethical reflection, decision-making, and change-making. papers.title: Enhancing Elementary Teachers’ AI-TPACK through a Professional Development Workshop
papers.authors: Ying-Tien Wu, Li-Jen Wang
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI presents new opportunities for personalized learning and adaptive instruction in elementary education. However, many teachers lack the necessary AI-TPACK competencies to integrate AI effectively. This study examines the impact of a two -day professional development workshop designed to enhance elementary educators' AI knowledge, pedagogical applications, and ethical awareness. Findings from pre - and post- workshop assessments indicate significant improvements in AI proficiency, instructional integration, and ethical considerations. Educators reported increased confidence in using AI for lesson planning and student engagement, yet highlighted the need for ongoing training in ethical AI use, privacy, and fairness. These results underscore the importance of structured, hands -on AI training to support responsible and effective AI integration in classrooms. Future research should explore long-term impacts on teacher engagement and student learning outcomes.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Enhancing Elementary Teachers’ AI-TPACK through a Professional Development Workshop. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Enhancing Teacher-AI Collaboration: The Impact of Prompt Engineering on Generative AI's
papers.authors: Ismail Celik, Kateryna Zabolatna, Olga Viberg
papers.abstract: Little is known about the instructional value of generative AI (GenAI) outputs in response to different prompts. This study designed prompts for ChatGPT based on the Knowledge Construction (KC) framework and evaluated outcomes in three subjects using the TPACK framework. Results show that higher KC phases produced more pedagogically meaningful outputs. “Integration of technology” and “student engagement” emerged as key usage aims, highlighting the importance of theory- informed prompt engineering in enhancing teacher-AI collaboration.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Effectiveness. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Evaluating Efficacy of Problematizing Chatbot in Higher Education
papers.authors: Tanmay Sinha
papers.abstract: Five graduate students brainstormed with a problematizing chatbot for project work. Reflections showed that despite some discomfort with persistent questioning, the brainstorming experience was rich and productive overall. Grading student chats showed high engagement but inadequate use of prompting strategies and weak critical analyses of AI -generated responses. Results implicate a greater focus on AI literacy training that facilitates knowledge of effective prompting and awareness of the limitations of generative AI to encourage critiquing its output.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Evaluating Efficacy of Problematizing Chatbot in Higher Education. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Developing a Generative AI Framework for Analyzing Student Responses to Enhance Classroom Assessments
papers.authors: Namsoo Shin, Yue Xing, Xunlei Qian, Joseph Krajcik
papers.abstract: This study develops and tests a Large Language Model -based AI framework for analyzing written responses on assessment tasks, generating scoring reasoning, and identifying response uncertainties to provide feedback that supports learning. Using prompt engineering and aggregation methods, the proposed AI models achieved an overall accuracy of 85% when scoring 834 written responses. These findings demonstrate the framework’s potential to enhance the rationale of classroom assessments by providing timely, feedback to improve teaching and learning. Objectives and conceptual framework Knowledge-in-use refers to students applying their knowledge with scientific practices to solve complex problems (Pellegrino & Hilton, 2012). Classroom assessments provide tangible evidence of this knowledge, enabling feedback to support learning (Harris et al., 2024). Timely, targeted feedback fosters cognitive growth by engaging learners to reflect on their knowledge, identify weaknesses, seek additional information, and revise their work (Nicol et al., 2006). Effective feedback should be based on analyzing student responses, making judgments about student performance, and providing clear, actionable feedback on areas for improvement to foster ongoing learning and growth. Yet, teachers have little time to provide such feedback. Advances in Generative AI (GenAI), notably Large Language Models (LLMs), facilitate automated analysis of written responses in assessment tasks to provide meaningful feedback. Chain- of-Thought (CoT) prompting (Wei, et al., 2022) enhances LLMs by breaking responses into critical components, identifying logical connections, and generating intermediate explanations to inform final scoring decisions. This approach highlights weaknesses or ambiguities in individual responses rather than relying on predefined or programmatic outputs. It provides personalized guidance that encourages learners to iteratively refine their answers to achieve their learning goals. This study aims to develop a GenAI- enhanced assessment framework to (1) analyze students’ written responses, (2) generate reasons for scoring decisions and identify response uncertainty, and (3) assign final scores and provide feedback on weaknesses to support learning. This study explores two research questions (RQs): RQ1, “How can AI algorithms, leveraging LLM and grounded in learning theories, be developed to analyze student responses and identify weakness in written responses for knowledge -in-use assessment tasks?” RQ2, “How can uncertainty in student responses be identified to provide feedback on knowledge -in-use assessment tasks?”
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Developing a Generative AI Framework for Analyzing Student Responses to Enhance Classroom Assessments. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Design-Based Research for Scenario-Based, Generative AI-Augmented Simulation in Nursing Education
papers.authors: Jinho Kim, Maria Feliciana Galindo-Parra, Seora Kim, Yoojin Bae, Terry Morris Hendry, Sujay Saphire Galen,
papers.abstract: Simulation-based learning is vital in  nursing education but  faces scalability and authenticity challenges. This study explores using generative AI as a role- playing agent in nursing simulations. Using a  design-based research approach, we developed an evaluation framework and question set to evaluate AI model performance. Findings highlight accurate role- based dialogue but limitations in common-sense reasoning. Recommendations include clearer evaluation criteria, diverse question sets to comprehensively evaluate ambiguity handling, and refining scenarios iteratively for consistency and clarity.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Design-Based Research for Scenario-Based, Generative AI-Augmented Simulation in Nursing Education Jinho Kim, Maria Feliciana Galindo-Parra, Seora Kim, Yoojin Bae, Terry Morris Hendry, Sujay Saphire Galen, Min Kyu. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Toward a Method for Visualizing Interactional Copresence
papers.authors: Katherine C. Chapman, Elizabeth Metts
papers.abstract: This poster presents a provocation for methodological advancements in qualitative inquiry into spatial pedagogy. Using classroom data that includes student talk during groupwork sessions and a dynamic map of teacher location, we offer several visualization s to invite speculation about how we might amend these tools to think more deeply about the joint accomplishment of copresence in classrooms. Overview Existing literature on spatial pedagogy predominantly originates in the field of learning analytics and tends to promote a cognitivist framework and/or an evaluative stance (e.g. Lim et al, 2012; Martinez- Maldonado et al, 2022). Researchers in the Learning  Sciences have made some movement toward promoting sociocultural perspectives on this emerging topic, as well as integrating it with teacher perspectives and issues of responsive teaching (Shapiro et al., 2024). Nevertheless, there is much to explore with regards to how concepts of space and place may be developed as an interactional achievement of people in classrooms, both for teachers concerned about spatial equity, and for researchers thinking about moving past analytic concepts like location and proximity and toward interactionist notions of copresence (c.f. Campos -Castillo & Hitlan, 2013). Furthermore, with the increasing prominence of computer -aided investigative tools, and particularly their utility in mapping space and movement, it behooves us as a field to think about how these complex, dynamic concepts can be embedded in tools that inherently privilege unitarily defined variables. In this poster, we present counter -intuitive examples and possible alternative uses of a GIS tool (described below) as provocations for considering methodological innovations in visualizing teacher -student copresence beyond simple proximity. We do so with illustrative data from an ongoing project involving this same tool. Even so, we are not making an argument about what these new visualizations do or do not show, only positing that such visualizations could help disturb the idea that location or proximity alone are the best window into the interactional accomplishment of thinking together in a classroom. This provocation contributes to the emerging focus of spatial pedagogy in the Learning Sciences, and particularly how an interactionist view can push this work without eschewing computerized tools. Theoretical orientations We take an interactionist view grounded in sociocultural theories of learning (Vygotsky, 1986) and building on the work of Lave and Wenger (1991), which holds that learning takes place in a community of practice that both shapes and is shaped by the actions of individuals in coordination with other people, as well as cultural tools and practices, as they work toward some goal. More specifical ly, we aim to connect this work to notions of placemaking (Zitcer, 2020) and to previous literature on copresence (Goffman, 1964; Campos -Castillo & Hitlan, 2013), highlighting how the subjective experience of being present with a more knowledgeable other (Moll, 1990) is intimately tied to temporally emergent routines and their attendant expectations and awareness patterns.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Toward a Method for Visualizing Interactional Copresence Katherine C. Chapman. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: BlockTalk: GenAI Simulations for Conversational Debugging Practice
papers.authors: Paulina Haduong, Brian Yu, Miranda Shen, Bobby Gerami, Karen Brennan
papers.abstract: Conversing with students about challenges is central to the work of teaching computing through opportunities to create self-directed and open-ended programming projects. We introduce BlockTalk, a generative AI tool for teachers to practice conversational debugging through simulations. Our exploratory analysis examines teachers’ interactions with the AI and offers insights for debugging pedagogy.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: BlockTalk: GenAI Simulations for Conversational Debugging Practice Paulina Haduong. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Identifying Challenges and Interaction Issues in a Generative AI-Assisted Code Description Activity for Programming Beginners
papers.authors: Muyang Wu, Sumin Hong, Ruiwei Xiao
papers.abstract: This study investigates the challenges programming beginners face when using Generative AI to describe coding intentions. We analyzed data from 120 students where students described problems, and AI generated code. Performance was evaluated across 48 tasks in eight categories using metrics. Our findings indicate that tasks in the “dictionaries” category are the most challenging for beginners. Additionally, we identified recurring interaction issues such as amb iguous instructions, assumptions about AI understanding, and misalignment with code logic.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Identifying Challenges and Interaction Issues in a Generative AI-Assisted Code Description Activity for Programming Beginners. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Theoretical Construction and Case Study of Temporal Learning Analytics Based on Learning Engagement Dynamics Framework
papers.authors: Hai Li, Zifeng Liu, Jie Chao, Wanli Xing
papers.abstract: Temporal learning analytics faces challenges of lacking systematic theoretical guidance and "black- box" feature extraction. This study proposes the learning engagement dynamics (LED) framework, decomposing digital learning behavior into three complementary, cognitively grounded dimensions: cognitive temporal regulation (CTR), task engagement dynamics (TED), and information exploration and integration (IEI), enabling a transparent mapping from clickstream data to cognitive constructs. In a theory- driven case study, we derived 16 temporal features and analyzed 837,144 interactions from 117 middle  school students in AI-literacy modules using cross-classified nested random-effects models. Findings: (1) CTR (behavioral regularity) shows significant associations with cognitive engagement; (2) TED signals relate positively to accuracy on structured tasks, suggesting the value of sustained deep engagement; and (3) IEI exhibits task- specific patterns, systematic exploration associates with improved accuracy, while broader exploration relates to potential interference. LED provides a theoretical foundation and preliminary empirical insights for personalizing intelligent learning platforms.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Theoretical Construction and Case Study of Temporal Learning Analytics Based on Learning Engagement Dynamics Framework. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Designing Transformational Games to Support Socio-ethical Reasoning about Generative AI
papers.authors: Jaemarie Solyst, Ruth Karen Nakigozi, Chloe Fong, R. Benjamin Shapiro
papers.abstract: There is an increasing need for young people to become critically AI literate, understanding not only how AI works but also its limitations and ethical nuances. Yet, designing learning experiences that make such complex, serious topics engaging remains a challenge. This paper explores transformational games  as a promising approach for supporting youth learning about generative AI (GenAI) and ethics. We designed and implemented two games, Diversity Duel and Secret Agent, that integrate GenAI tools with gameplay elements. This work investigates how the games’ elements: (1) peer evaluation, (2) constraint -based creativity, and (3) social deduction supported socio- ethical reasoning about GenAI. Participants recognized and debated bias in GenAI outputs, connected these patterns to real -world inequities, and developed nuanced understandings of bias. Participants further came to see how prompt design shapes AI behavior. Our findings suggest that group- based games with these elements can support fostering critical AI literacy.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Designing Transformational Games to Support Socio-ethical Reasoning about Generative AI. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and education.

papers.title: Shared Epistemic Agency in K-12 AI-Infused Lesson Planning: Exploring Human-AI Collaboration in Designing Pedagogically Meaningful Learning Experiences
papers.authors: Yingru Zhao, Haesol Bae, Jaesung Park, Devan Walton, Raymond Weiss
